global temperature.name: Global Temperature
global temperature.description: Rising long-term temperature changes the baseline that weather now operates on, making heat extremes, heavy rainfall, and stress on ice, crops, and ecosystems more likely.
incoming: Carbon dioxide traps heat that would otherwise escape to space. As emissions accumulate in the atmosphere, global temperatures rise.

Methane traps heat very effectively, so releasing more of it raises global temperatures, especially over the next few decades. Cutting methane emissions can therefore slow near-term warming faster than reductions in longer-lived gases alone.

Reduced marine low-cloud cover reflects less sunlight and amplifies warming. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assesses the subtropical marine low-cloud feedback as positive with high confidence.

Declining reflective aerosol forcing removes part of the historical masking of greenhouse-gas warming. Human-caused aerosols exert a net negative heat-trapping influence, so reducing that negative forcing can add near-term warming unless greenhouse-gas forcing falls sufficiently at the same time.
Land carbon sink weakening amplifies temp by leaving more emitted carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of land carbon sink weakening.

Ocean carbon uptake weakening amplifies temp by increasing the airborne fraction of carbon emissions. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of ocean carbon uptake weakening.

Removing forest changes water loss from soil and plants, latent and sensible heat, roughness, turbulent mixing, absorbed solar radiation and heat storage locally, while atmospheric and oceanic adjustments create nonlocal responses. Forest-carbon loss adds a separate greenhouse-gas warming process.

Nitrous oxide absorbs heat in the atmosphere and remains there for a long time, adding to global warming alongside carbon dioxide and methane. Its long atmospheric lifetime and strong infrared absorption add a warming influence, contributing to warming alongside other greenhouse gases.

A change in reflected sunlight or trapped infrared energy alters the planetary energy budget. The temperature response can be warming or cooling and must retain the observed shortwave, longwave, and net signs.
A positive forcing adds energy to the climate system. Surface and ocean warming proceed until radiative feedbacks and heat uptake move the system toward a new balance.

Some observed stratospheric smoke episodes produced a net short-lived cooling influence, but composition, altitude, lifetime, clouds, and surface surface reflectivity determine the sign and magnitude. Limited to the documented affected system and exposure footprint.
outgoing: Warmer air can contain more water vapour, increasing moisture convergence and event-scale precipitation intensity when lifting and storm dynamics are present. Additional warming increases the moisture ceiling available to the heaviest precipitation events.

Warming can increase ecosystem respiration, drought and fire losses and thaw frozen carbon, raising natural net carbon release or weakening uptake. This is a carbon-climate feedback, not the original human-caused emissions driver.

Warming can enhance microbial methane production in waterlogged wetlands and can expose thawed permafrost carbon. The net atmospheric response depends on hydrology, oxidation, transport and concurrent human-caused emissions.
A warmer atmosphere and ocean hold more heat and moisture. This makes extreme heat, heavy rain, drought, and several hazards happening together more likely.

A warmer baseline raises both heat and atmospheric moisture capacity, making dangerous heat-humidity combinations more likely and pushing wet-bulb exposure closer to physiological limits. Within tropical land regions between 20 degrees South and 20 degrees North, climate models constrained by atmospheric dynamics project regional extreme wet-bulb temperature to rise with tropical-mean warming.

Rising temperatures alter land-ocean thermal contrast and moisture loading, which can destabilize monsoon timing and rainfall intensity even though regional circulation details still matter. Warming and greenhouse-gas forcing can intensify persistent hot-night exposure and alter drought or monsoon characteristics, but the sign, magnitude and event definition remain region-, season- and mechanism-specific.

Rising surface temperatures increase active-layer depth and thaw frozen ground, making permafrost thaw one of the clearest direct frozen-water system responses to planetary warming. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.

Warming shifts winter precipitation from snow toward rain and increases midwinter melt, raising the chance of rain-on-snow runoff and flood damage in cold regions. Warming can increase rain-on-snow flood risk in snow-covered basins by raising freezing levels, shifting winter precipitation toward rain, and accelerating melt when rain, snow-water equivalent, soil saturation, and basin routing align.

Warming initially raises glacier meltwater production but continued ice loss reduces glacier area, so many glacier-fed basins ultimately pass a runoff maximum and enter declining long-term meltwater contribution. Warming alters glacier and sea-ice energy balance, ocean heat and freshwater structure, and carbon uptake.

Warming shifts precipitation phase and accelerates snow loss, making higher temperature an upstream driver of snow-drought risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Higher temperatures can reduce takeoff performance and amplify runway and operations stress, making warming an upstream pressure on airport climate exposure. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.

Urban tree canopy can decline under rising heat, drought stress, and compounding urban pressures, especially where maintenance and water access lag. Global Temperature raises pressure on through heat and drought stress.

Higher air temperatures increase surface melting, while ocean warming can erode floating ice shelves and speed the discharge of grounded ice into the ocean. Compiles satellite observations of Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet mass loss.

As air warms it can hold more water vapor, so rising temperature is a direct upstream driver of humidity amplification and compound heat stress. Global Temperature increases as warmer air supports more atmospheric moisture.

Warming increases evaporative demand and can deepen atmospheric dryness even before rainfall deficits fully emerge at the surface. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.
Lightning Ignition under Fire Weather Conditions

Hotter, drier, more unstable conditions can raise ignition-prone fire weather and help align lightning with receptive fuels. Warming can worsen the conditions under which lightning ignites and sustains wildfire by increasing heat and atmospheric drying, but it does not determine lightning occurrence or ignition by itself.

Higher temperatures can intensify wildfire conditions and extend smoke seasons, increasing the burden of smoke exposure. Warming can increase wildfire-smoke exposure where it lengthens or intensifies fire seasons and smoke reaches populated areas.

Hot, sunny conditions can accelerate photochemical reactions and increase some precursor emissions while stagnant air limits dilution, raising episode potential where reactive gases are present. Warmer sunny conditions can increase the photochemical pressure for ground-level ozone formation where nitrogen-oxide and reactive-organic precursors are available, while transport and chemical regime determine the realized concentration.

Human-caused warming shifts daytime maxima and nighttime minima upward, increasing compound day-night heat extremes. Warming and greenhouse-gas forcing can intensify persistent hot-night exposure and alter drought or monsoon characteristics, but the sign, magnitude and event definition remain region-, season- and mechanism-specific.

Human-caused warming has increased nighttime heat stress risk by raising minimum temperatures and humid-heat exposure. Warming and greenhouse-gas forcing can intensify persistent hot-night exposure and alter drought or monsoon characteristics, but the sign, magnitude and event definition remain region-, season- and mechanism-specific.

Surface warming changes marine low-cloud controlling factors and is assessed to produce a positive subtropical low-cloud feedback. Global warming can reduce marine low-cloud amount in susceptible subtropical regimes through boundary-layer, inversion, moisture and circulation responses.

Ocean warming lowers the amount of oxygen water can hold and strengthens ocean layering and reduces ventilation that drive deoxygenation. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Ocean warming and added freshwater from land-ice loss strengthen density differences between surface and deeper water, limiting vertical mixing and reinforcing salinity-driven layering that limits mixing. Warming alters glacier and sea-ice energy balance, ocean heat and freshwater structure, and carbon uptake.

Southern Ocean warming and freshening contribute to weaker dense-water formation, with regional variability and multiple controls. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.

Upper-ocean warming strengthens density layering that limits mixing and can reduce vertical mixing, especially in coastal and shelf systems already sensitive to ventilation loss. Warming and freshening strengthen density layering in coastal and shelf waters, reducing vertical mixing, oxygen renewal, and resilience against low-oxygen events.

Warming changes freezing levels and convective environments, redistributing hail hazard rather than uniformly increasing it everywhere. Global warming redistributes hail-prone conditions poleward through competing changes in instability, melting level, moisture and wind shear.

Warmer upper-ocean water supplies more heat and moisture to an organized tropical cyclone, creating conditions that can help it strengthen very quickly. If winds and storm structure are favorable, that extra energy can support rapid intensification before landfall.

Higher global temperatures change river-flow timing and volume through evaporation, precipitation, snowmelt, and runoff timing. That can move peak flows earlier, deepen low-flow periods, and make water supplies less predictable.

Higher temperatures and more intense heat events increase heat-related mortality risk, especially when exposure and vulnerability are already high. Extreme heat becomes a mortality burden when exposure, age, chronic illness, housing, and care-system access combine beyond safe recovery limits.
Rising heat and humidity reduce safe labor capacity and increase work-related heat strain across exposed sectors. Global Temperature raises through higher heat and humidity during working hours.

Higher global temperatures intensify wildfire risk and behavior through hotter, drier, and longer fire-weather conditions. Fires can then ignite more easily, spread faster, and burn across a longer season.
Higher global temperatures raise port heat vulnerability through worker, equipment, and pavement heat stress. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Higher air temperature and solar heating raise steel-rail temperature and compressive stress, increasing buckling risk when track temperature exceeds the range supported by rail stressing, track form and maintenance condition. Research supports this direct process: temp raises risk of rail_heat_buckling through rail thermal expansion.
Through hotter growing-season conditions, Global Temperature increases Farm Heat Stress. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.
Higher global temperatures shift livestock disease pressure through heat stress and changing pathogen and vector ranges. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Higher global temperatures add pressure toward insect biomass decline through heat extremes and climate-driven habitat disruption. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Higher global temperatures melt Arctic sea ice earlier and delay its return in autumn, shortening the annual sea-ice season. At stabilized global warming of 2 degrees Celsius, the assessed annual probability of a practically sea-ice-free Arctic September by the end of the century is 10-35 percent, compared with approximately 1 percent at 1.5 degrees Celsius.
Loss of Firn Meltwater Storage Capacity

Higher global temperatures accelerate firn layer depletion through greater surface melt and reduced refreezing capacity. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of warming.

Temperature affects vector and pathogen biology, shifting transmission suitability within disease-specific thermal limits. Temperature changes can alter vector survival, development, biting rates, pathogen incubation, season length, and geographic suitability.
Higher global temperatures contribute to land carbon sink weakening through heat, drought, fire, and respiration effects. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Warming raises surface-ocean surface-ocean carbon dioxide pressure, lowers carbon dioxide ability to remain dissolved, and strengthens layering that limits mixing, reducing uptake and exchange with the ocean interior. Ocean warming reduces carbon-dioxide ability to remain dissolved and contributes to physical feedbacks that weaken ocean sink efficiency.

A warmer atmosphere can intensify short-duration rainfall extremes, making temperature an upstream driver of flash-flood regime change. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.
Warmer air pulls more water from soil and plants. Where rain does not replace that loss, drought can become more severe and last longer.

Warming and drying pressure raise watershed forest stress by increasing fire exposure, water loss from soil and plants pressure, and hydrologic instability across forested basins. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Higher global temperature raises sea level by expanding ocean water and accelerating land-ice melt, making warming a direct upstream driver of coastal inundation risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Hotter conditions speed soil organic matter breakdown and weaken moisture retention, making warming an upstream pressure on humus decline. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Warming melts reflective snow and sea ice, exposing darker surfaces that absorb more solar energy and reinforce additional melt. Warming alters glacier and sea-ice energy balance, ocean heat and freshwater structure, and carbon uptake.

Warming advances snowpack disappearance and can shift precipitation from snow to rain in temperature-sensitive mountain regions. Warming can reduce mountain snowpack and advance melt and runoff timing, especially where winter precipitation falls near the rain-snow transition.

Global warming is expressed faster in the Arctic because sea ice, snow, clouds, and heat transport feedbacks amplify regional temperature change above the global mean. Warming alters glacier and sea-ice energy balance, ocean heat and freshwater structure, and carbon uptake.

Contemporary warming can accelerate western-pine-beetle development and reduce larval overwinter mortality. During severe drought, weakened ponderosa-pine defenses allow the larger beetle population to translate that thermal response into additional overstory mortality.

Warmer seawater holds less dissolved oxygen, can increase organism and microbial oxygen demand, and can strengthen or prolong density layering that limits mixing that limits ventilation of bottom waters. These processes can increase oxygen stress in susceptible coastal waters, while nutrient loading, circulation and runoff remain independent and often dominant controls.

Ocean warming lowers seawater density and expands the ocean volume, raising global mean thermosteric sea level. Total sea-level rise also contains land-ice, land-water-storage, circulation, salinity and local vertical-land-motion terms that must remain separate.

Higher ambient temperature increases physiological heat load and can aggravate cardiovascular, renal, respiratory and thermoregulatory stress. Population deaths or years of life lost depend on the local nonlinear exposure-response curve, humidity, age, housing, health, cooling access and adaptation.

Warming and associated humidity, precipitation, sea-level and chloride-exposure changes alter carbonation, corrosion initiation and material deterioration rates. For reinforced concrete and steel assets this can shorten modeled service life and increase maintenance or failure risk.

Temperature variability and exposure above crop-specific optima affect phenology, reproductive success, water demand and extreme-heat damage. These processes can change interannual yield variability, but the sign differs where cold limitation eases, irrigation buffers heat, or other weather variables dominate.
Higher temperatures draw more water from soil and plants. When rain cannot replace that loss, large areas can enter severe soil-moisture drought.

Warming reduces seasonal sea-ice coverage and extends navigable periods in parts of the Arctic, enabling more shipping where infrastructure, economics and safety allow. Higher global temperatures can condition arctic shipping expansion through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.

Warmer air causes snow to melt earlier, shifting the spring runoff peak and changing when rivers receive water from the seasonal snowpack. Across 2,339 snow-affected, minimally impaired Northern Hemisphere catchments, a 1 degree Celsius increase in catchment annual mean air temperature was associated on average with a 4.7-day advance in the annual maximum snowmelt-flood peak date, with a 5.0-day cross-catchment standard deviation.

Warming thaws ice-rich permafrost, causing the ground to subside and expanding thermokarst pits, lakes and unstable terrain. Higher global temperatures can condition thermokarst expansion through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.

Warming retreats glaciers and can enlarge unstable meltwater lakes, increasing outburst-flood risk where moraine or ice dams are weak. Higher global temperatures can condition glacial lake failure risk through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.
Higher air and ground temperatures lengthen the thaw season and accelerate microbial activity in tundra soils. Waterlogged, oxygen-poor areas can then release more methane to the atmosphere.

Warming changes snow accumulation, layering and the frequency of rain or meltwater entering the snowpack. These shifts can weaken mountain snow stability and alter avalanche timing near transport passes.
Atmospheric and ocean warming increase surface and basal melt around Antarctic outlet glaciers. Thinning near the grounding zone can move the point where grounded ice begins to float farther inland.
Warming thins Arctic sea ice and reduces the mechanical resistance of the pack. Thinner, more fragmented ice responds more readily to winds and currents, changing drift speed and direction.
Warmer glacier surfaces increase melt around dark cryoconite sediment. Localized absorption deepens and widens melt holes when debris remains concentrated and sunlight is available.
Temperature controls meltwater availability, brine structure and light conditions within snow and sea ice. Warming can shift the timing, habitat and visible pigment concentration of ice-algae blooms.
Warming increases glacier melt and can enlarge or destabilize water stored within and beside glaciers. Sudden drainage from those reservoirs produces high-volume outburst floods.

Sustained warming raises the equilibrium snowline and increases melt across an ice cap’s summit. Once the highest accumulation area disappears, the remaining cap loses its long-term refuge from net melt.

Warming can expand surrounding ice-free terrain in some places but also removes persistent snow and cold microclimates used by nunatak specialists. Habitat shrinks where heat, exposure and competing species exceed their tolerances.

Warmer coastal water allows some disease-causing microbes, including Vibrio bacteria, to survive in more places and for longer periods. Atmospheric warming raises coastal water temperature, altering the environmental envelope for temperature-sensitive marine pathogens such as Vibrio.

Warmer air and sea temperatures promote ground thaw and thermal abrasion, increasing susceptibility to wave-driven erosion where ice-rich shorelines are exposed. Arctic coasts underlain by thawing permafrost can erode rapidly as warmer ground, sea-ice loss, and wave attack destabilize bluffs, roads, settlements, and shore infrastructure.

Global and regional warming condition Antarctic shelf instability through Southern Ocean warming and, in some locations, enhanced surface melt and hydrofracture risk. How strongly this effect develops depends on regional ocean circulation, surface melt and firn state, and ice shelf geometry.

Repeated crossings around freezing can make water in existing fractures expand and contract, producing stress and incremental movement. How strongly this effect develops depends on cycle duration, temperature range, and rock type.

Hot, sunny, stagnant conditions often accelerate photochemistry and favor accumulation, while the response still depends on precursor supply, clouds, mixing, and transport. Warming can modify habitat suitability, forest stress, ozone-forming conditions and aquatic oxygen loss, but each outcome requires additional biological, chemical or land-management conditions and must not be inferred from temperature alone.

Water entering fractures can deepen cracks and destabilize already vulnerable floating or marine-terminating ice. Warming alters glacier and sea-ice energy balance, ocean heat and freshwater structure, and carbon uptake.

High ambient air temperature raises winding hot-spot temperature and reduces the equipment ability to shed internally generated heat, accelerating insulation aging and increasing abrupt-failure risk. The relationship is limited to the stated mechanism, geography, time, and measurement boundary.

Warming can make formerly unsuitable habitat climatically accessible, alter seasonal survival, and change the effectiveness of controls, allowing some established non-native populations to expand. Warming can reduce suitability for some invaders.

Higher temperature increases evaporative demand and can intensify moisture stress, interacting with rainfall change, fire, and land use to favour lower-biomass vegetation. Temperature alone does not determine biome state, and projected transition thresholds remain uncertain.

Warmer seasonal conditions and later first frost can lengthen the period during which allergenic plants flower and pollen remains detectable. Warmer seasonal temperatures and more frost-free days can lengthen ragweed pollen season by shifting flowering and the first fall frost.

Higher land temperature and water loss from soil and plants can intensify moisture stress and erosion risk, interacting with precipitation change and management to degrade dryland soil and vegetation. Some drylands may receive more rain or show vegetation gains, and attribution requires multiple land-condition indicators.

This allows atmospheric rivers to carry more moisture and produce heavier rain when their wind pattern remains similar. Atmospheric warming increases column-integrated water vapor, allowing a circulation feature with comparable winds and geometry to transport more moisture and produce higher rain rates.
Convective Available Potential Energy and Inhibition Anomaly

A warmer, moister lower troposphere can make a lifted parcel more buoyant relative to its environment and increase potential updraft energy, while changes aloft and convective inhibition can offset or delay release. Surface warming alone does not determine parcel buoyancy.
Lightning Flash Density and Seasonality Anomaly

Warming changes buoyancy, moisture, precipitation, and mixed-phase cloud processes that control electrification, but different physically plausible parameterizations produce different regional and global signs. Cloud-resolving studies show that widely used proxies can predict substantially different future signs, and global models have little consensus because electrification and graupel are represented incompletely.
Migratory Bird Timing, Route, and Stopover Disruption

Changing temperature and precipitation can advance spring conditions and food phenology, while populations using photoperiod, distant conditions, or inherited schedules may respond at different rates, altering passage dates and resource overlap. Responses vary among species and sites, some populations track resources or benefit from longer seasons, and an early year does not establish a forced trend or mismatch.
Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction

Higher temperature can reduce snow storage, advance melt, raise atmospheric water demand, and alter competitive limits, causing mortality or failed regeneration at dry margins even while cold-limited upper boundaries may expand. Warming can permit upslope establishment in cold-limited locations, and temperature alone does not establish net contraction without moisture, disturbance, regeneration, and both boundary directions.
Amphibian Chytrid Infection Prevalence and Mortality

Environmental temperature shapes fungal growth and host-pathogen interaction, with field evidence showing highest infection at intermediate conditions and lower prevalence or intensity at both colder and hotter ends. The relationship is hump-shaped rather than monotonic, host species differ strongly, and warming may reduce suitability at hot sites while increasing it at formerly cold sites.
North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre Circulation Strength

Warmer or less strongly cooled surface water remains lighter, reducing deep mixed-layer formation and altering isopycnal slopes and geostrophic pressure gradients that contribute to the cyclonic flow. Temperature alone cannot determine density or circulation, regional warming can be advected by stronger flow, and a cold surface anomaly may result from atmospheric heat loss rather than weakened transport.

Warmer growing seasons can increase development rates and voltinism, while reduced winter mortality allows larger populations to reach mass-attack thresholds. Excessive heat can reduce survival, and warming does not increase outbreaks where hosts or suitable moisture are absent.

Warmer water holds less oxygen and can strengthen layering that limits mixing, increasing hypoxia risk where nutrient loading and weak mixing are already present. Warming can modify habitat suitability, forest stress, ozone-forming conditions and aquatic oxygen loss, but each outcome requires additional biological, chemical or land-management conditions and must not be inferred from temperature alone.

Warming raises heat, aridity, and drought stress and increases the probability of crossing uncertain regional dieback thresholds. Warming can modify habitat suitability, forest stress, ozone-forming conditions and aquatic oxygen loss, but each outcome requires additional biological, chemical or land-management conditions and must not be inferred from temperature alone.

Arctic warming can lengthen growing conditions and favor expansion of some shrub species, although species traits, moisture, snow, herbivory, and disturbance shape the local response. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.

Heat and climate-driven range or phenology changes can stress susceptible pollinators, but local land use, pathogens, pesticides, and forage remain important co-drivers. Agricultural pesticide and habitat pressures or climate stress can contribute to pollinator population or colony loss, but each process must be tied to a named pollinator, exposure window and demographic outcome within a multistressor system.

Warming can increase evaporative demand and alter snowmelt and runoff timing, changing stored surface-water availability in susceptible basins. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.

Sustained ground warming can enlarge zones that remain unfrozen within or beneath permafrost, with snow, water, soil, and vegetation controlling local development. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.
Warming can reduce performance and persistence at warm range margins. When colonization at cooler margins cannot compensate, the occupied range contracts.

human.summary: Global warming raises heat exposure, reduces safe outdoor work hours, increases drought and flood losses, and makes more neighborhoods costly to cool or protect.
consequences: Heat illness, kidney stress, and excess mortality rise during longer hot seasons.
Crop yields and livestock productivity fall as heat stress compounds drought.
Cooling demand and utility bills climb fastest in already heat-exposed cities.
human.hiddenCost: Each increment of global warming increases losses and damages across health, food, water, infrastructure, and ecosystems; those costs are not contained in the price of the emissions that cause them.
human.whoPays: People and regions with the least adaptive capacity, including low-income communities and climate-sensitive livelihoods, experience disproportionate losses despite contributing less to cumulative emissions.

planet.summary: Global temperature rise destabilizes multiple Earth systems at once by accelerating ice loss, ocean heat stress, biodiversity decline, and hydrologic disruption.
consequences: Heat stress pushes species beyond historical thermal niches and compresses viable habitat.
Snow, glacier, and sea-ice loss alter reflectivity and freshwater timing across regions.
Ocean and land systems both experience more frequent threshold-like stress events.
planet.physicalLimit: There is no single global economic cliff at one temperature. The physical constraint is a finite cumulative carbon budget: stabilizing human-caused warming requires net-zero anthropogenic carbon dioxide emissions.

response.defaultDriver: Continued net greenhouse-gas emissions from fossil energy, land-use change, infrastructure lock-in, and delayed investment keep adding warming and future adaptation costs.
levers: Cutting greenhouse-gas emissions rapidly across energy, land, transport, buildings, and industry.
Reaching net-zero carbon dioxide while reducing non-CO2 forcing to stabilize warming.
Directing adaptation finance and resilient infrastructure toward populations with the highest exposure and lowest adaptive capacity.

measurement.metric: Global mean surface temperature anomaly above 1850-1900
measurement.unit: degrees Celsius
measurement.geography: global with land-ocean coverage diagnostics
measurement.cadence: monthly with annual synthesis
measurement.method: Use the published global surface-temperature anomaly; retain baseline, coverage, land-ocean method, provisional status, and ensemble or dataset spread. Do not substitute a satellite atmospheric-layer temperature.
measurement.uncertainty: Coverage, homogenization, sea-surface-temperature methods, baseline conversion, and provisional recent observations produce dataset spread.
measurement.boundary: Retain the latest annual reviewed value and mark stale when the source is unavailable; never infer missing months from the TULIP score.

methane emissions.name: Methane Emissions
methane emissions.description: Methane is a powerful heat-trapping gas, so leaks from fossil systems and emissions from agriculture can speed up near-term warming.
incoming: Warming can enhance microbial methane production in waterlogged wetlands and can expose thawed permafrost carbon. The net atmospheric response depends on hydrology, oxidation, transport and concurrent human-caused emissions.

When thawed permafrost becomes waterlogged and oxygen-poor, microbes convert stored carbon into methane that can escape into the atmosphere. Permafrost thaw is a well-established methane-release feedback.

Food waste disposed in landfills decomposes anaerobically and produces methane, making this a direct waste-management emissions process. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of food waste.
Flooded rice fields create oxygen-poor soil where microbes produce methane. The gas then escapes through rice plants, bubbles, and the water surface.
Through thawed, waterlogged carbon decomposition, Thermokarst Expansion can increase Methane Emissions. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of thermokarst expansion increases.

Methane Leak Detection and Repair reduces Methane Emissions when observations trigger verified repair. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Methane produced in thawing tundra soils, wetlands and lakes can escape into the atmosphere when microbial production exceeds oxidation. The added methane strengthens near-term warming, although flows vary sharply with soil moisture, temperature and transport processes.
Livestock, manure, rice, and other intensive agricultural practices can release methane. The magnitude depends on production system and management.

Expansion of unfrozen, permeable processes beneath thawing terrain or lakes can enable methane production and release where organic carbon and low-oxygen conditions are present. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.

Anaerobic decomposition of liquid manure produces methane unless gas is captured and destroyed or used. Apply only within the named basin, airshed, production system, or humanitarian response context.

More ruminants generally increase total enteric methane within the herd boundary, while diet and productivity alter emissions per animal and per unit product. Apply only within the named basin, airshed, production system, or humanitarian response context.
outgoing: Methane traps heat very effectively, so releasing more of it raises global temperatures, especially over the next few decades. Cutting methane emissions can therefore slow near-term warming faster than reductions in longer-lived gases alone.

Methane traps substantially more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide over the near term, adding warming that can intensify heat, rainfall and other climate extremes. Co-occurring or sequential heat, heavy-rainfall, drought, wildfire, cyclone, and flood hazards.

Methane adds to the near-term warming burden that raises humid heat exposure. Combined heat and humidity extremes push human survivability limits, reduce labor capacity, and strain power, health, and cooling systems during prolonged heat events.

Methane emissions add strong near-term warming, changing atmospheric moisture and circulation in ways that can alter monsoon timing and rainfall variability. Erratic monsoon onset, breaks, and retreat intensify flood-drought swings, destabilizing food production, water storage, and hydro-dependent economies.
More methane uses up chemicals in the air that normally help remove it. With less of this natural cleaning capacity available, methane can remain in the atmosphere longer.
Higher globally averaged abundance increases direct forcing and also affects ozone and stratospheric water vapour. Overlap with other absorbers is included in the assessment method.

human.summary: Methane speeds up near-term warming, making heat, crop losses, and ozone-related respiratory harm arrive sooner.
consequences: Extra warming amplifies dangerous heat seasons within policy and infrastructure timescales.
Methane-driven ozone damages crops and increases breathing conditions in polluted regions.
Food-price volatility rises when heat and ozone reduce agricultural output together.
human.hiddenCost: The costs created by Methane Emissions are not fully reflected when decisions omit its effects on health, livelihoods, and essential services and on atmospheric chemistry and climate stability.
human.whoPays: People and ecosystems exposed to Methane Emissions bear the greatest burden where protection, alternatives, monitoring, or recovery capacity are limited.

planet.summary: Methane speeds up near-term planetary heating and increases ozone damage, feedback risk, and ecosystem stress on timescales short enough to outrun slow adaptation.
consequences: Fast warming raises the chance of crossing ecological thresholds before recovery buffers can respond.
Ozone damages plant tissue and suppresses photosynthesis in crops and wild vegetation.
Methane growth compounds cryosphere and permafrost feedback risks.
planet.physicalLimit: The relevant constraint is Anthropogenic methane emissions by source sector, measured within its declared geography, period, and uncertainty rather than assumed from the label alone.

response.defaultDriver: Atmospheric methane remains a high-leverage warming gas.
levers: Prevent Methane Emissions at its source through enforceable emissions, discharge, product, or process standards.
Measure Anthropogenic methane emissions by source sector at the facilities and places where exposure or ecological damage can occur.
Require cleanup, repair, or safer substitution when monitoring shows Methane Emissions exceeds the declared threshold.

measurement.metric: Anthropogenic methane emissions by source sector
measurement.unit: million tonnes CH4 per year

measurement.uncertainty: Emission factors, activity data, super-emitters, wetlands, source attribution, atmospheric transport, and inventory revisions affect totals.
measurement.boundary: Do not convert concentration growth directly to anthropogenic emissions without an atmospheric budget and sink estimate.

deforestation.name: Deforestation
deforestation.description: Forest loss removes carbon storage, dries out landscapes, weakens rainfall cycles, and leaves soils and species more exposed.
incoming: Verified clearing of prior forest for subsequent oil-palm establishment is a direct agricultural land-use conversion and therefore a defined component of deforestation. Tree-cover loss or later oil-palm presence alone is insufficient.

High-volume, short-use fashion demand can increase procurement of new leather and bio-based fibres. Where bovine leather originates from cattle expansion in a forest-risk frontier, or forest-derived cellulosic fibre lacks deforestation-free traceability, clothing and footwear demand can transmit commodity pressure into forest conversion.

Demand for cattle, feed, oil crops and other agricultural commodities can increase production incentives and land requirements. Where yield growth, intensification, trade, governance or use of existing cleared land do not absorb that demand, producers can expand pasture or cropland by converting forest to agricultural land.

Horizontal expansion of settlements, roads and urban infrastructure can replace forest with built land, producing permanent land-use conversion. Outward expansion of settlements and infrastructure can permanently convert forest to built land and therefore cause a bounded share of deforestation.
Forests are permanently converted to cropland or pasture to expand agricultural production. Agricultural expansion for cropland and livestock is the dominant direct global driver of deforestation.

Mine footprints and associated infrastructure remove forest cover and open previously inaccessible forest to additional land conversion. Mining can directly clear forest at extraction sites and indirectly expand forest loss through access roads, settlements, and induced activity.
outgoing: Forest clearing fragments habitat when it divides previously contiguous forest into smaller or more isolated patches and increases edge exposure. Research supports this direct process: deforestation creates forest_fragmentation when clearing divides contiguous habitat.
Deforestation directly weakens land carbon sink weakening by removing biomass and degrading soils. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of deforestation.

Forest clearing and fragmentation remove food, shelter and stable microclimates for insects, reducing biomass where remaining habitat cannot support viable populations. Deforestation removes forage, nesting space, and microclimate stability, making it an upstream driver of insect biomass decline.

Removing forest cover exposes soil to erosion, heat and faster organic-matter breakdown, gradually reducing the humus that supports fertility and water retention. Deforestation strips litter inputs, canopy protection, and root structure from soils, accelerating the loss of humus and other organic matter.

Fragmentation and forest degradation can reduce resilience to heat, drought, pests, and fire, contributing to dieback where these stressors coincide. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Forest clearing and fragmentation reduce water loss from soil and plants and moisture recycling, expand edges, and increase fire incidence. These effects can combine with climate change to favour a persistent lower-biomass state.

Removing forest changes water loss from soil and plants, latent and sensible heat, roughness, turbulent mixing, absorbed solar radiation and heat storage locally, while atmospheric and oceanic adjustments create nonlocal responses. Forest-carbon loss adds a separate greenhouse-gas warming process.

Large-scale forest removal changes surface reflectivity, surface roughness, water loss from soil and plants and moisture recycling. The resulting land-temperature and hemispheric-energy contrasts can alter pressure gradients, cross-equatorial flow, monsoon circulation and rainfall.

Forest conversion changes canopy, light, temperature, standing water, predators, host communities and human contact patterns. In some tropical settings these changes favor mosquito species that transmit human pathogens, increasing vector abundance or richness and creating conditions that can support disease emergence or geographic expansion.

Clearing forest within a watershed removes canopy and root structure, reducing forest cover while increasing erosion and rapid runoff into streams. Deforestation can condition watershed forest loss through the reviewed biodiversity mechanism.

Clearing peatland vegetation commonly accompanies drainage and land conversion, disrupting hydrology, exposing peat, and removing the plant community that sustains peat formation. Promoted from exact-term ontology research only within the documented mechanism and scope.
Forest removal changes interception, rooting, soil structure, water loss from soil and plants, and runoff. In documented settings faster surface runoff reduces water reaching recharge zones.

Forest conversion and fragmentation alter host communities and edges between natural and settled land, creating new contact opportunities through which a pathogen may cross species and later transmit among people. Most land conversion does not produce an outbreak, and causation requires pathogen, host, exposure, and transmission evidence rather than spatial coincidence.

Forest clearance releases carbon stored in trees and soils while removing a living carbon sink. Emissions rise further when vegetation is burned or decomposes, and future carbon uptake falls when forest becomes pasture or cropland.

Forest loss can alter water loss from soil and plants, infiltration, and water regulation, increasing water-stress risk where forest-water functions are material. Persistent imbalance between water demand and available supply raises the baseline fragility of cities, farms, power systems, and river ecosystems.
Population and Asset Exposure in Floodplains
Forest loss can increase downstream sediment and flood risk where watershed routing and exposed people or assets are present. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Forest conversion and fragmentation remove habitat and can reduce biodiversity intactness in the affected landscape. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Forest loss and degradation can interact with drying and ignition to alter fire regimes. Climate, fuels, and management moderate the outcome.
Removal of forest cover can reduce soil protection and increase erosion under erosive rainfall and slope conditions. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Forest loss can degrade water quality, flow regulation, and habitat, stressing freshwater ecosystems under documented catchment conditions. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Loss of forest-derived livelihoods and ecosystem services can contribute to displacement pressures alongside economic, political, and climatic drivers. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Forest and semi-natural habitat loss can reduce floral resources, nesting sites, refugia, and connectivity, contributing to pollinator population or colony loss alongside pesticides, pathogens, climate, and management. Named pollinator population or managed colony system within a mapped forest and semi-natural-habitat landscape.

human.summary: Forest loss removes rainfall buffering, destabilizes water supplies, and undermines food, income, and safety for communities that depend on intact landscapes.
consequences: Dry-season fires and smoke raise respiratory illness and destroy homes and assets.
Rainfall becomes less reliable as forest moisture recycling weakens.
Loss of forest income, fuelwood, and flood buffering pushes households into deeper insecurity.
human.hiddenCost: Forest conversion removes biodiversity, carbon storage, water regulation, and livelihood services whose losses are only partly reflected in agricultural, timber, mining, or infrastructure revenues.
human.whoPays: Indigenous Peoples, forest-dependent communities, downstream water users, and climate-exposed populations bear losses in livelihoods, cultural systems, water regulation, and resilience.

planet.summary: Deforestation fragments habitat, weakens carbon sinks, alters rainfall recycling, and reduces whole-biome resilience.
consequences: Species lose connected habitat and face rising extinction risk as landscapes are fragmented.
Forest-rainfall feedbacks weaken, making dry seasons longer and ecosystems more fire-prone.
Carbon sink capacity declines as mature canopy is replaced by degraded or cleared land.
planet.physicalLimit: There is no universal hectare threshold for forest-system collapse. Recovery depends on biome, fragmentation, fire, soil condition, climate, and whether ecological connectivity and regeneration capacity remain.

response.defaultDriver: Agricultural expansion is the dominant global direct driver, interacting with commodity demand, infrastructure, mining, weak land governance, insecure tenure, and enforcement gaps.
levers: Decoupling agricultural commodity production from forest conversion through traceable supply chains and enforceable land-use rules.
Securing Indigenous and community land rights and strengthening monitoring and enforcement where conversion pressure is high.
Protecting intact forests while restoring degraded land without treating plantations as equivalent to natural forest ecosystems.

measurement.metric: Forest conversion and annual forest-area change
measurement.unit: hectares per year and percent of baseline forest area
measurement.geography: bounded region first; aggregate only with reviewed spatial weights
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to source release
measurement.method: Normalize forest conversion and annual forest-area change against a fixed, source-appropriate baseline; preserve source flags and spatial coverage.
measurement.uncertainty: Preserve source uncertainty, sampling and model limitations, revisions, and geographic coverage; do not infer missing observations as zero.
measurement.boundary: Retain the last reviewed value, mark it stale, expose the failed source and coverage, and do not update graph scores.

industry farming.name: Industry Farming
industry farming.description: Industrial farming drives up fertilizer use, water demand, and land stress, which can increase emissions, pollute waterways, and weaken soil health.
incoming: Demand growth is met partly through yield, stocking, and production-intensity increases when land expansion, imports, or demand reduction do not absorb it. Growth in demand for food, feed, fibre, and animal-source products increases pressure for higher-output and more intensive agricultural production systems.

Commercial livestock systems concentrate production by relying on larger and more standardized flows of maize, soy, protein meal, and other feed crops. Expansion of compound-feed-dependent livestock production is a major process of agricultural intensification.

External nutrient inputs raise attainable yields and support repeated high-output cropping where soil nutrients would otherwise constrain production. Availability and use of synthetic fertilizer is an enabling input for input-intensive crop-yield intensification.
outgoing: Irrigated agriculture is a major basin-scale withdrawal pressure, so intensive farming is an upstream contributor to baseline water stress. Persistent imbalance between water demand and available supply raises the baseline fragility of cities, farms, power systems, and river ecosystems.

Groundwater depletion is a direct process where irrigation and farm withdrawals outpace recharge over years to decades. Aquifers are being drawn down faster than they recharge, turning hidden water reserves into a long-lived constraint on farming, drinking water, and ecosystem resilience.

Industrial farming increases nutrient runoff risk because concentrated fertilizer use often outruns field uptake and enters waterways. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.
Industry farming can embed irrigation water inefficiency through poorly matched application and conveyance losses. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.
Industry farming can accelerate soil humus decline through intensive disturbance and low organic-matter return. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of industry farming increases.
Industry farming can accelerate topsoil erosion acceleration through intensive tillage and exposed soil. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.

Industry farming can contribute to insect biomass decline through habitat simplification and intensive chemical exposure. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of industry farming.

Dependence on synthetic fertilizer exposes industrial farming to natural-gas prices, trade restrictions and supply disruptions that can rapidly raise input costs. Input-intensive industrial farming is directly exposed to fertilizer price shocks because nutrient costs feed quickly into planting decisions and food-system margins.

Concentrated livestock production creates sustained demand for maize, soy and other feed crops, tying animal output to cropland, fertilizer, water and trade. Industrial livestock systems deepen dependence on feed-crop supply chains that transmit land, water, and fertilizer stress through animal production.

High stocking pressure and repeated trampling, especially on wet soils, can compact rangeland and pasture soils. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.
Persistent Pesticide Residues in Sediment and Biota

Historical or current agricultural use can load persistent compounds into watershed soils and sediments, which may expose aquatic organisms and consumers long after the original application. Most pesticide mass applied in agriculture is not necessarily persistent or bioavailable, and current land use cannot identify the source of a legacy compound without historical and chemical evidence.

Crop-protection chemicals applied to fields can dissolve in water, bind to eroded particles, move through tile drains, or leach and discharge to streams. The process depends strongly on the compound and management.
Agricultural pesticide application can generate airborne droplets or dust that move off target during or shortly after spraying. Some active ingredients can also volatilize and move later.
Forests are permanently converted to cropland or pasture to expand agricultural production. Agricultural expansion for cropland and livestock is the dominant direct global driver of deforestation.
Industrial farming can release nitrous oxide when manure and crop residues add nitrogen to soil or are burned. Soil microbes convert some of that nitrogen into this powerful greenhouse gas.
Flooded rice production creates anaerobic soil conditions in which organic matter decomposes and produces methane. This edge is limited to the rice-cultivation component of the wider sector.

Commercial plantation establishment directly converts prior land cover when industrial cultivation expands onto forested parcels. The process depends on verified pre-plantation forest and does not apply to replanting or expansion on non-forest land.
Expanding or poorly managed farmland can strip away plant cover, erode soil, drain groundwater, and leave salt behind. Over time, the land becomes less able to support crops and ecosystems.

Agricultural disturbance and poor land management can strip vegetation or break surface structure, increasing wind erosion from otherwise vulnerable dry soil. Agriculture can reduce rather than increase erosion when protective cover, windbreaks, reduced tillage, and appropriate grazing are used.

Cropland expansion, livestock pressure, fuel management, and deliberate clearing can reduce woody cover when they overlap mapped savanna vegetation. Named agricultural frontier or rangeland with dated land-cover and management evidence.

High animal density, repeated contact, movement through production chains, and inadequate biosecurity can increase pathogen maintenance, evolution, worker exposure, or transmission through contaminated food. Intensive production with effective biosecurity can reduce some exposure routes, and the direction differs by pathogen and production system.
Livestock, manure, rice, and other intensive agricultural practices can release methane. The magnitude depends on production system and management.

Land conversion, energy use, and agricultural inputs can add carbon emissions within the stated accounting boundary. Crop and livestock activity within a declared farm-gate boundary emits methane and nitrous oxide, while marine-fuel combustion emits carbon dioxide within declared total- or international-shipping boundaries.

Habitat simplification, pesticides, nutrient loading, and land conversion can reduce biodiversity intactness where those pressures are documented. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Nutrient losses from intensive agriculture can contribute to coastal hypoxia where downstream transport, loading, and oxygen response are documented. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
Agricultural nutrient loading can contribute to oxygen-depleted coastal zones where the receiving-water mechanism is measured. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Monoculture, habitat loss, and pesticide exposure can reduce pollinator resources and services, subject to local management and landscape context. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Input dependence, soil degradation, and water stress can increase food-security risk when yields, prices, or access are affected. Uncertain or constrained physical and economic access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food.
High disturbance, low-diversity rotations, and chemical or nutrient pressures can alter soil biological communities. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Agricultural burning, ammonia, and other emissions can contribute to air-pollution burdens under documented emission and exposure conditions. Ambient ozone, particulates, and combustion by-products translate transport and industrial activity into chronic respiratory, cardiovascular, and mortality risk.

Pesticide exposure, habitat simplification, and reduced floral diversity can contribute to colony losses, alongside pathogens, parasites, nutrition, and weather. Agricultural pesticide and habitat pressures or climate stress can contribute to pollinator population or colony loss, but each process must be tied to a named pollinator, exposure window and demographic outcome within a multistressor system.

Input-intensive crop production can increase fertilizer application, while crop choice, precision management, and soil fertility determine actual rates. Synthetic or organic nitrogen applied to managed soils within a named crop, area, and reporting period.

Concentrated livestock systems may use liquid manure storage, but system design and regional regulation determine whether lagoons are present. Operation of a named manure lagoon, bounded by animal type, manure loading, retention time, temperature, treatment state, and reporting period.

Concentrated livestock production can raise animal density within a managed area, subject to land availability and husbandry system. Documented cattle liveweight or animal units per paddock area and grazing interval.

human.summary: Industrial farming concentrates food output, pollution, labor exposure, and animal disease risk into a single system that can fail expensively for both producers and consumers.
consequences: Nutrient runoff contaminates rivers and raises drinking-water treatment burdens.
Workers and livestock face heat stress that cuts productivity and raises mortality risk.
Fertilizer, feed, and disease shocks translate quickly into food-price increases.
human.hiddenCost: Greenhouse-gas and nitrogen emissions, land-use change, water withdrawals, pollution, unhealthy diets, and social vulnerability create agrifood-system costs that market food prices do not fully represent.
human.whoPays: Farm workers, small producers, low-income consumers, downstream water users, and low-income countries carry disproportionate health, livelihood, pollution, and price-shock burdens.

planet.summary: Industrial farming drives nutrient overload, soil degradation, biodiversity simplification, and freshwater ecosystem stress.
consequences: Nutrient runoff fuels algal blooms and oxygen depletion in downstream waters.
Monoculture landscapes reduce pollinator diversity and ecological redundancy.
Repeated extraction lowers soil organic matter and long-term land resilience.
planet.physicalLimit: There is no single global intensity threshold. Production is constrained by locally finite soil, freshwater, nutrient-loading, biodiversity, and heat limits, with strong crop and regional variation.

response.defaultDriver: Input subsidies, procurement and commodity incentives, concentrated supply chains, dietary demand, and prices that omit environmental and health costs reward throughput over resilience.
levers: Reducing nitrous oxide from fertilizer, methane from livestock and rice, and carbon losses from soils with measured, place-specific management.
Reforming support and procurement so soil, water, health, and biodiversity outcomes affect production incentives.
Reducing food loss and waste and shifting demand where doing so lowers land, water, and emissions pressure without worsening nutrition or livelihoods.

agricultural demand.name: Agricultural Demand
agricultural demand.description: Diet compares familiar foods directly, so users can see how beef, dairy, poultry, grains, and plant proteins differ on the same food-footprint scale.
incoming: The Indian Ocean Dipole can bring drought to some farming regions and heavy rain to others. Harvest impacts depend on where crops are grown and how farms prepare.
Livestock disease pressure disrupts food through mortality, reduced productivity, and movement controls. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of livestock disease pressure.
Fertilizer price shock raises pressure on food through higher input costs and constrained production. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of fertilizer price shock increases.
Agricultural labor exposure reduces reliability of food through heat-related labor capacity loss. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of agricultural labor exposure.
Feed crop dependency transmits risk into food when feed shortages constrain livestock production. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of feed crop dependency.
Cold chain failure risk reduces usable supply of food through spoilage and unsafe storage. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of cold chain failure risk.

El Niño-related heat, drought and flooding can reduce harvests and interrupt food supplies in exposed production regions. This edge represents El Niño–Southern Oscillation-related crop and fishery disruption processes into food-system stress.

La Niña can bring destructive rainfall to some farming regions and drought to others, disrupting harvests, fisheries and the reliability of regional food supplies. This edge captures El Niño–Southern Oscillation-linked agricultural and fishery stress processes into food volatility.

Extreme heat and humidity reduce safe working hours for farm labor and can stress crops and livestock, lowering food production in exposed regions. This edge captures labor productivity loss and crop stress under combined heat-humidity extremes.

Unreliable monsoon timing and rainfall disrupt planting, irrigation and harvests, reducing agricultural output where food production depends heavily on the seasonal rains. Monsoon volatility is a direct process into food-production disruption.
outgoing: Food moving through production, storage, distribution, retail, and consumption creates stage-specific opportunities for loss and waste. It is not a fixed conversion of demand into waste.

Demand for cattle, feed, oil crops and other agricultural commodities can increase production incentives and land requirements. Where yield growth, intensification, trade, governance or use of existing cleared land do not absorb that demand, producers can expand pasture or cropland by converting forest to agricultural land.

Demand for agricultural commodities induces production and supply-chain activity. Fossil fuels and fossil-generated electricity used for machinery, fertilizer manufacture, processing, refrigeration, transport and retail emit carbon dioxide.

Demand for high crop yields drives production of nitrogen, phosphate and potash fertilizers used to replenish nutrients removed during harvest. Industrial fertilizer production ties fossil gas, ammonia synthesis, nitrous oxide risk, and runoff-intensive farming systems together.

Demand growth is met partly through yield, stocking, and production-intensity increases when land expansion, imports, or demand reduction do not absorb it. Growth in demand for food, feed, fibre, and animal-source products increases pressure for higher-output and more intensive agricultural production systems.

Sustained demand for rice can expand or intensify flooded cultivation, increasing the activity base when yields, trade, diets, and water availability do not offset the response. Crop, water regime, and management remain explicit.

Demand for edible oils and palm-containing food and consumer products can increase production and land demand. Forest clearance occurs only where added supply is met through plantation expansion into forest rather than yield gains, replanting, stocks, substitution, or expansion on already-cleared land.

human.summary: Agricultural demand hits people when food systems overuse land and water, making diets more expensive and supply chains more fragile.
consequences: Staple and protein prices rise when demand growth outruns climate-stressed supply.
Cropland and grazing expansion intensify land clearing and water withdrawals.
Import-dependent populations face sharper food-security shocks during harvest failures.
human.hiddenCost: Global food demand externalizes health costs through diet-related diseases and the destruction of carbon-rich forests.
human.whoPays: Taxpayers fund government health budgets, while rural communities pay with degraded local water and air.

planet.summary: Global agricultural demand for food, particularly meat and dairy.
consequences: Demand for cattle, feed, oil crops and other agricultural commodities can increase production incentives and land requirements.
Demand for agricultural commodities induces production and supply-chain activity.
planet.physicalLimit: Converting natural land to crops triggers regional dryland desertification as local moisture loops break.

response.defaultDriver: Global supply chains prioritize low-cost animal proteins and processed grains, locking consumers into high-footprint defaults.
levers: Restructuring agricultural subsidies to disincentivize intensive livestock feed crops and reward low-footprint protein diversification.
Implementing land-protection mandates that block supply chain financing for commodities grown on deforested or conversion-exposed soils.
Diverting institutional procurement budgets toward local, regeneratively grown, plant-centric foods.

measurement.metric: Apparent domestic agricultural commodity demand
measurement.unit: tonnes per year by commodity with kilograms per person reported separately
measurement.geography: country or declared market region
measurement.cadence: annual
measurement.method: Calculate production plus imports minus exports and stock additions under a declared commodity balance; retain food, feed, seed, processing, and loss uses separately.
measurement.uncertainty: Informal trade, stock changes, commodity conversion, feed allocation, waste, and statistical revisions affect apparent demand.
measurement.boundary: Do not add commodities with incompatible mass equivalents or equate apparent supply with consumption.

urbanization.name: Urbanization
urbanization.description: Urban expansion replaces vegetated land with heat-absorbing surfaces, raising heat exposure, runoff, and flood risk.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Urban growth can expand built area and housing footprints where development takes a low-density or outward-growth form. Legacy edge upgraded with relationship-specific authoritative evidence and bounded scope.

Population and economic growth can raise municipal demand faster than sources, networks, treatment, and loss control expand, increasing the likelihood of intermittent supply or scheduled restrictions during scarcity. Urban growth need not produce rationing when supply, reuse, efficiency, and infrastructure keep pace.

Urbanization simultaneously changes population density, household size, buildings, transport, public infrastructure, industrial structure, income, technology, land cover and energy intensity. These processes can raise or lower territorial carbon emissions, and spatial spillovers can transfer part of the response to adjacent regions.

Horizontal expansion of settlements, roads and urban infrastructure can replace forest with built land, producing permanent land-use conversion. Outward expansion of settlements and infrastructure can permanently convert forest to built land and therefore cause a bounded share of deforestation.

Urban population growth, construction, consumption and industrial concentration can raise blue-water demand and grey-water pollution pressure within and beyond administrative boundaries. Agglomeration, industrial restructuring, infrastructure and water-efficiency improvements can moderate or reverse the net effect at higher development levels.

Urban population, income and business activity can increase demand for air travel, provided fares, airport capacity and alternatives do not offset that growth. Urbanization can condition aviation demand growth through the reviewed infrastructure mechanism.

Urban growth concentrates food retail, restaurants and households, increasing potential waste volumes while logistics and collection systems determine how much is actually discarded. Loss and disposal across farms, retailers, kitchens, and landfills turn food systems into avoidable methane, water, and land-use pressure.

Urban growth adds cooled floor area and heat-retaining surfaces, increasing demand for air conditioning and its associated refrigerant stock. Cooling systems combine growing electricity demand with potent refrigerant leakage, making heat adaptation itself part of the climate story.

Dense populations, artificial containers, drainage gaps, mobility, and uneven vector control can increase vector-human contact and transmission persistence. Rapid or poorly serviced urbanization can expand habitat, host density, water-storage practices, and exposure networks favorable to some disease vectors.

Impervious urban drainage can route more rapid runoff into a combined sewer, raising overload pressure where capacity and storage are limited. Applies only where a combined sewer system and a documented overflow process exist.

Impervious surfaces, engineered drainage, and stream diversion can move precipitation rapidly to surface channels instead of allowing infiltration through recharge zones. Leaking utilities, recharge basins, and stormwater infiltration can locally maintain or increase recharge.

Development can remove habitat and introduce physical and behavioral barriers, collision risk, noise, light, and hostile land cover that reduce successful movement and gene flow between remaining patches. Some urban green spaces and backyards provide usable links, crossing structures can restore permeability, and urban presence alone does not establish a barrier for every species.

Concentrated human activity combines abrasion, material handling, waste, road dust, and repeated surface disturbance, increasing the opportunity for small polymer particles to enter and re-enter near-surface air. Remote deposition is well documented, an urban site can receive transported particles, and a land-use gradient alone does not identify the emitting activity.

Piers, seawalls, aquaculture gear, and other hardened surfaces can provide attachment habitat for benthic polyps that produce free-swimming medusae. Named developed coast with comparable artificial and natural substrate surveys.

Expansion into natural or peri-urban habitat, altered waste and food systems, animal movement, and dense human contact networks can change spillover opportunity and onward transmission after introduction. Urban growth alone does not identify the reservoir, exposure route, or outbreak source, and improved services can lower disease risk.

Growth in buildings and infrastructure can increase demand for conventional cement and concrete, moderated by material efficiency, reuse, and construction standards. Cement and concrete lock construction demand into kiln heat, limestone heating emissions, quarrying, and long-lived material throughput.

Population and built-area growth can increase simultaneous municipal demand, moderated by efficiency, pricing, climate, and network design. Measured peak demand above a named utility’s available supply or treatment capacity.

human.summary: Urban expansion can trap people in hotter, flood-prone places when housing, drainage, trees, and transit lag behind population growth.
consequences: Neighborhood heat and flood exposure rise when paving outpaces cooling and drainage.
Water, sanitation, and transport systems are strained by dense growth without resilience upgrades.
Housing costs and displacement pressures increase around rapidly expanding urban cores.
human.hiddenCost: The costs created by Urbanization are not fully reflected when decisions omit its effects on health, livelihoods, and essential services and on climate, ecological, and resource systems.
human.whoPays: People and ecosystems exposed to Urbanization bear the greatest burden where protection, alternatives, monitoring, or recovery capacity are limited.

planet.summary: Urbanization can affect atmospheric chemistry and climate stability, biodiversity, habitat, and ecosystem resilience, and freshwater timing, quality, and aquatic habitat through Carbon Emission, Deforestation, and Baseline Water Stress.
domains: freshwater timing, quality, and aquatic habitat
consequences: Urbanization simultaneously changes population density, household size, buildings, transport, public infrastructure, industrial structure, income, technology, land cover and energy intensity.
Horizontal expansion of settlements, roads and urban infrastructure can replace forest with built land, producing permanent land-use conversion.
Urban population growth, construction, consumption and industrial concentration can raise blue-water demand and grey-water pollution pressure within and beyond administrative boundaries.
planet.physicalLimit: The relevant constraint is Annual expansion of built-up surface, measured within its declared geography, period, and uncertainty rather than assumed from the label alone.

response.defaultDriver: The conversion of rural landscapes into dense urban settlements.
levers: Address the verified upstream pressures that increase Urbanization rather than treating the observed outcome in isolation.
Use Annual expansion of built-up surface to test whether policy or operational changes are reducing the condition.
Direct protection and investment toward the people, infrastructure, and ecosystems most exposed to Urbanization.

measurement.metric: Annual expansion of built-up surface
measurement.unit: hectares per year with urban population share reported separately
measurement.geography: urban centre, metropolitan area, country, or declared grid
measurement.cadence: annual to multi-year remote-sensing update
measurement.method: Classify built-up surface using a fixed GHSL product and boundary; compare harmonized epochs and retain population, density, redevelopment, and boundary-change diagnostics.
measurement.uncertainty: Sensor resolution, classification, settlement boundary, vertical development, informal settlements, cloud, and epoch spacing affect expansion estimates.
measurement.boundary: Do not count administrative boundary expansion as physical urbanization or infer land conversion between incompatible product versions.

fast fashion.name: Fast Fashion
fast fashion.description: High water use, petrochemical inputs, dye pollution, and waste give low-cost, short-lived clothing an impact that extends far beyond the store.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: Fast fashion is linked to emissions through energy-intensive manufacturing and logistics. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of fast fashion.

Rapid clothing turnover increases demand for fibres, water, energy and chemical processing, accelerating resource use before garments reach the end of their practical life. This edge captures textile water demand and pollution pressure.

High-volume, short-use fashion demand can increase procurement of new leather and bio-based fibres. Where bovine leather originates from cattle expansion in a forest-risk frontier, or forest-derived cellulosic fibre lacks deforestation-free traceability, clothing and footwear demand can transmit commodity pressure into forest conversion.
High-volume textile production and short product lifetimes increase wastewater, dye, chemical, and waste burdens. The receiving-water effect depends on treatment and disposal controls.

human.summary: Fast fashion shifts water pollution, waste, and labor harm onto communities far from the checkout counter.
consequences: Untreated textile effluent contaminates local rivers used for drinking and irrigation.
Low-wage supply chains concentrate occupational exposure and wage vulnerability.
Disposable clothing volumes overwhelm waste systems and increase toxic burning and dumping.
human.hiddenCost: Cheap polyester clothes release microplastics into our water systems that cannot be captured by standard filters.
human.whoPays: Water companies pay more to filter municipal supplies, while communities near textile dumps absorb toxic waste fumes.

planet.summary: Fast Fashion can affect atmospheric chemistry and climate stability and biodiversity, habitat, and ecosystem resilience through Carbon Emission, Resource Depletion, and Deforestation.
consequences: Fast fashion is linked to emissions through energy-intensive manufacturing and logistics.
Rapid clothing turnover increases demand for fibres, water, energy and chemical processing, accelerating resource use before garments reach the end of their practical life.
High-volume, short-use fashion demand can increase procurement of new leather and bio-based fibres.
planet.physicalLimit: Synthetic fibers do not biodegrade, and mechanical recycling degrades them into smaller microplastics that shed faster.

response.defaultDriver: Fast fashion profit models rely on rapid turnover and low-cost petroleum-derived synthetic fabrics.
levers: Imposing extended producer responsibility (EPR) fees at the point of sale to finance textile recycling.
Enforcing strict microplastic filtration standards on industrial and household washing machines.
Mandating durability and chemical labeling standards on all imported apparel.

measurement.metric: Textile products placed on market and unsold textiles destroyed
measurement.unit: tonnes per year, reported separately
measurement.geography: declared facility, industry class, country, trade region, or supply-chain boundary
measurement.cadence: monthly or annual according to production and inventory reporting
measurement.method: Retain product, process, material, energy, emissions, water, and waste boundaries; normalize by output only when numerator and denominator share the same facility, geography, and period.
measurement.uncertainty: Confidential reporting, facility coverage, process heterogeneity, trade allocation, emission factors, and inventory revisions affect estimates.
measurement.boundary: Do not infer facility performance from national averages or merge production, footprint, and intensity into one value.
