delta salt intrusion fronts.name: Delta Salt Intrusion Fronts
delta salt intrusion fronts.description: Salt fronts can push farther inland in deltas and estuaries as sea level rises, river discharge weakens, and storm-driven water levels press saline water into farms and intakes.
incoming: Higher coastal water levels allow saline water to penetrate farther inland through estuaries, deltas, and connected coastal aquifers, especially during low-flow periods. Salt fronts can push farther inland in deltas and estuaries as sea level rises, river discharge weakens, and storm-driven water levels press saline water into farms and intakes.

When river discharge weakens or shifts seasonally, freshwater resistance to estuarine salinity intrusion drops and inland salt fronts can move farther upstream. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of river flow regime change.

Prolonged drought reduces river flow and estuarine flushing, allowing saline fronts to penetrate farther inland and persist longer. Extends when prolonged low-flow conditions allow saline fronts to move farther inland.
outgoing: Salt intrusion can threaten freshwater intakes and raise treatment difficulty, forcing utilities to manage salinity spikes, blending limits, and intake shifts. Threatens when saline water intrudes into source intakes and treatment systems.
Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands

Advancing saline fronts and tidal pressure can intensify intrusion into shallow coastal freshwater bodies, thinning already vulnerable freshwater lenses. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of delta salt intrusion fronts increases.

Salt-front migration is a practical process into coastal aquifer degradation because it increases salinization pressure in connected estuarine and delta groundwater systems. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of delta salt intrusion fronts.

extreme precipitation intensity.name: Extreme Precipitation Intensity
extreme precipitation intensity.description: A warmer atmosphere can dump more water in short bursts, increasing the intensity of rainfall events that overwhelm drainage, utilities, and river management systems.
incoming: Warmer air can contain more water vapour, increasing moisture convergence and event-scale precipitation intensity when lifting and storm dynamics are present. Additional warming increases the moisture ceiling available to the heaviest precipitation events.
The Madden-Julian Oscillation changes tropical winds and moisture. In some places and seasons, those shifts can make heavy rain more likely or more intense.

Moisture amplification supplies more condensable water to organized convection, fronts, and other lifting systems. Higher event-available atmospheric moisture raises potential rainfall totals and intensities when precipitation is triggered.

Seasonal wind and moisture-transport departures alter convergence, active-break timing, and the location of intense monsoon rainfall. Large monsoon circulation and moisture-transport anomalies can concentrate rainfall into more extreme regional events.
Carbon-dioxide emissions warm the atmosphere, increasing the amount of water vapor it can hold. When storms have sufficient lift and moisture supply, that higher ceiling allows heavier precipitation.
Greater integrated vapor transport and longer duration deliver more moisture to a region. Orographic or frontal ascent can convert that flow into higher and more persistent rain or snow rates.
Convective Available Potential Energy and Inhibition Anomaly

Greater parcel buoyancy can support faster updrafts and stronger condensation and precipitation production, but realized totals and rates depend on moisture supply, initiation, entrainment, microphysics, motion, and organization. High potential energy can remain capped or produce little rain, while extreme rain can occur in low-energy but very moist or strongly forced environments.

Compound climate hazards can include heavy-precipitation episodes where atmospheric conditions produce extreme rainfall. A warmer atmosphere can dump more water in short bursts, increasing the intensity of rainfall events that overwhelm drainage, utilities, and river management systems.
outgoing: Heavier short-duration rainfall increases flash-flood risk when rainfall rates overwhelm local drainage, infiltration, and channel capacity. More intense short-duration precipitation can increase the frequency or magnitude of pluvial and flash flooding when rainfall rates exceed local infiltration, channel, storage or artificial-drainage capacity.

More intense short-duration precipitation can exceed sewer conveyance and treatment-system design capacity, increasing overflow risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of extreme precipitation intensity.

Intense rainfall can overwhelm runway drainage, reduce visibility and force ground stops, producing airport delays and cancellations. Extreme precipitation intensity can condition airport operational disruption through the reviewed infrastructure mechanism.

Heavy rainfall and runoff can freshen the ocean surface locally, strengthening short-lived layering that limits mixing when winds and mixing remain weak. Extreme precipitation intensity can condition ocean salinity layering that limits mixing through the reviewed oceans mechanism.

Storm environments capable of intense precipitation can also support damaging hail, but hail size and frequency depend on updraft strength, freezing level and wind shear. Hail hazard shift is included as a distinct severe-convective climate signal because the Nature Climate Change study links warming to a redistribution of hail-prone environments and associated crop risk.
Intense rainfall increases runoff entering a combined sewer. Overflow occurs when that runoff exceeds the system capacity.

Heavy rain and rapid snowmelt can supply water to joints where subsequent freezing, thawing, and pore pressure weaken susceptible blocks. How strongly this effect develops depends on rainfall timing, drainage, and fracture aperture.

Intense rainfall can raise outwash and delta discharge, mobilizing fine material and episodically introducing coarser loads. How strongly this effect develops depends on antecedent storage, grain size, and delta geometry.

Floodwater and high river flow can remove pipeline cover, erode crossings, overwhelm containment, or move released material rapidly into a channel. How strongly this effect develops depends on crossing depth, bank erosion, and secondary containment capacity.

Heavy rainfall can raise discharge, erode recently exposed sediment and channel banks, and compound melt-driven transport in glaciated basins. How strongly this effect develops depends on antecedent melt, vegetation cover, and slope stability.

Intense rainfall and flood peaks can increase near-bank shear stress, toe scour, saturation, and mass failure in susceptible reaches. Named river reach with rainfall, discharge, bank geometry, substrate, and repeat surveys.

Heavy warm rainfall onto an existing snowpack can combine rainfall runoff with rapid snowmelt, producing enhanced flood risk in snow-covered basins. Warming shifts cold-season storms toward rain falling onto existing snowpack, producing rapid runoff pulses, flood surges, and operational stress for mountain basins.

tropical cyclone rapid intensification.name: Tropical Cyclone Rapid Intensification
tropical cyclone rapid intensification.description: Warmer ocean conditions and favorable atmospheric setups can increase the likelihood that tropical cyclones intensify quickly before landfall, compressing preparation time and raising surge risk.
incoming: Warmer upper-ocean water supplies more heat and moisture to an organized tropical cyclone, creating conditions that can help it strengthen very quickly. If winds and storm structure are favorable, that extra energy can support rapid intensification before landfall.

Persistent anomalously warm surface water and associated upper-ocean heat can sustain air-sea heat and moisture transfer and limit storm-induced cooling, increasing the conditional likelihood of rapid intensification when wind shear, humidity, storm structure, and track are also favorable. Within the Gulf of Mexico and northwestern Caribbean study domain, qualifying marine heatwaves were associated with a higher conditional probability of tropical-cyclone rapid intensification, averaging 1.5-fold and reaching up to 5-fold in identified hotspot regions.

High tropical-cyclone heat potential provides a deeper warm reservoir, allowing strong air-sea heat transfer as the cyclone mixes the upper ocean. Deep upper-ocean heat reduces storm-induced cooling and sustains energy flow during rapid intensification.

Higher environmental and inner-core moisture limits dry-air disruption and supports sustained convective heating around the vortex. A moist storm environment supports organized deep convection and latent-heat release needed for intensification.

Carbon-dioxide emissions add ocean and atmospheric heat that can provide more energy for tropical cyclones. In otherwise favorable conditions, warmer upper-ocean water increases the potential for rapid intensification.

Compound climate hazards can include rapidly intensifying tropical cyclones only in storm-prone basins with suitable ocean and atmospheric conditions. steel.name: Steel
steel.description: Ore extraction, blast-furnace coal use, high-temperature heat, and construction demand combine into a concentrated industrial footprint.
incoming: No incoming relationship is asserted in the current reviewed graph.
outgoing: The steel transition gap reflects the difficulty of moving an energy- and coal-intensive material system onto lower-emissions production routes fast enough. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of steel production increases.

Sulfur-bearing feedstocks, coke combustion, and associated high-temperature processes can release the gas at iron and steel facilities unless captured or treated. Fuel sulfur, feedstock, process, and abatement determine magnitude.

Conventional iron and steel production releases carbon dioxide from fuel, reductant, and process energy use within the production boundary. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assesses global steel-production emissions at 3.7-4.1 GtCO2-equivalent in 2019, depending on the accounting scope.
Conventional production requires large flows of ore, reductants, energy, and other materials. Efficiency, recycling, and lower-impact processes moderate demand.

human.summary: Steel underpins buildings, transport, and energy infrastructure, but conventional production concentrates occupational hazards, hazardous air pollutants, and a large climate burden around long-lived industrial facilities.
consequences: Coke ovens, blast furnaces, foundries, rolling mills, and recycling operations require operation-specific worker protection and exposure control.
Integrated mills emit regulated metal and organic hazardous air pollutants that require source-specific controls.
The cost and timing of replacing long-lived blast-furnace assets shape how workers and industrial regions experience decarbonization.
human.hiddenCost: Conventional steel prices do not fully represent climate damages, hazardous emissions, or the transition risk embedded in long-lived coal-based production assets.
human.whoPays: Steelworkers and nearby communities face production hazards and air pollution, while industrial regions, consumers, and public budgets share the cost of replacing or retrofitting high-emission capacity.

planet.summary: Conventional steel production links coal-intensive iron reduction, high-temperature energy demand, mining inputs, and process emissions to a large global industrial footprint.

Scrap-based electric furnaces reduce energy demand, but scrap availability and quality constrain how far secondary production can substitute for primary steel.

Scaling hydrogen direct-reduced iron, low-emission electricity, and other near-zero primary-steel routes with the infrastructure they require.
Creating credible demand for near-zero-emission steel through standards, procurement, product definitions, and investment timed to plant replacement cycles.

incoming: Crop Yield Volatility increases the need for Climate-Resilient Agriculture as heat, water, pest, and market shocks become harder to absorb. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.
outgoing: Climate-Resilient Agriculture reduces Crop Yield Volatility through diversification, soil health, water management, and climate information. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Climate-Resilient Agriculture reduces Topsoil Erosion Acceleration through cover, roots, reduced disturbance, and water retention. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Climate-Resilient Agriculture can reduce Aquifer Overdraft when water efficiency is paired with basin withdrawal limits. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Climate-Resilient Agriculture can reduce Food Import Exposure by making domestic production more reliable across shocks. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

planned relocation.name: Planned Relocation
planned relocation.description: A rights-based path out of places that cannot be protected safely can preserve housing, livelihoods, culture, services, and community choice.
incoming: Managed Retreat Pressure increases the need for Planned Relocation when protection and repeated rebuilding no longer provide safety. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

aquifer overdraft.name: Aquifer Overdraft
aquifer overdraft.description: Groundwater withdrawal that exceeds the rate at which an aquifer can recharge. Sustained pumping can draw saline groundwater upward or inland; repeated use of mineralized irrigation water then leaves salts in the root zone as water evaporates or is taken up by crops.
incoming: Irrigation water inefficiency intensifies aquifer overdraft when avoidable losses are replaced through pumping. Low irrigation application or conveyance efficiency can increase gross groundwater withdrawals and contribute to aquifer overdraft where pumping persistently exceeds recharge and return flows.

Water Reuse and Recycling reduces pressure on Aquifer Overdraft when reuse displaces groundwater withdrawals. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Climate-Resilient Agriculture can reduce Aquifer Overdraft when water efficiency is paired with basin withdrawal limits. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Sustained groundwater withdrawals that exceed natural or managed recharge turn wider resource pressure into measurable aquifer overdraft. Aquifer overdraft is a direct resource-depletion process where extraction continues past recharge for years or decades.
outgoing: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands

Overpumping lowers freshwater heads and makes small-island lenses more vulnerable to saltwater intrusion and usable-storage loss. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of aquifer overdraft.
Pumping above recharge depletes groundwater storage and lowers water availability in monitored wells. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of aquifer overdraft.
Overpumping coastal aquifers lowers freshwater heads and increases depletion and saltwater-intrusion pressure. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of aquifer overdraft increases.
Sustained pumping can draw saline groundwater upward or inland. Repeated use of mineralized irrigation water then leaves salts in the root zone as water evaporates or is taken up by crops.

human.summary: Aquifer Overdraft can affect water security and sanitation and food security and livelihoods through Drinking Water Treatment Stress and Crop Yield Volatility.
consequences: Overpumping lowers freshwater heads and makes small-island lenses more vulnerable to saltwater intrusion and usable-storage loss. Downstream changes in Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands can then affect water security and sanitation through Drinking Water Treatment Stress.

Overpumping coastal aquifers lowers freshwater heads and increases depletion and saltwater-intrusion pressure. Downstream changes in Coastal Aquifer Salinization can then affect water security and sanitation through Drinking Water Treatment Stress.

Sustained pumping can draw saline groundwater upward or inland; repeated use of mineralized irrigation water then leaves salts in the root zone as water evaporates or is taken up by crops. Downstream changes in Topsoil Salinization Fields can then affect food security and livelihoods through Crop Yield Volatility.
human.hiddenCost: Excessive groundwater pumping permanently collapses underground aquifers, ruining soil storage capacity even if heavy rains return.
human.whoPays: Small farmers are ruined as water tables drop below shallow wells, leaving them with no water.

river flow regime change.name: River Flow Regime Change
river flow regime change.description: A persistent departure in river flow regime from its earlier pattern or state. When river discharge weakens or shifts seasonally, freshwater resistance to estuarine salinity intrusion drops and inland salt fronts can move farther upstream.
incoming: Higher global temperatures change river-flow timing and volume through evaporation, precipitation, snowmelt, and runoff timing. That can move peak flows earlier, deepen low-flow periods, and make water supplies less predictable.

Snowmelt timing shift advances river flow regime shift by moving runoff away from historical seasonal timing. Earlier snowmelt can shift snow-fed river flow toward earlier seasonal runoff and reduce warm-season contribution where storage and rainfall do not compensate.
Through reduced and earlier snowmelt runoff, Snow Drought intensifies River Flow Regime Change. Rivers then receive a smaller, earlier spring pulse and less water during the warm season.

Glacier outburst floods release stored meltwater abruptly, producing discharge peaks far above normal seasonal flow. Repeated drainage events can shift the timing, magnitude and sediment load of downstream river flow.

Storage, diversion, and operating rules can suppress seasonal peaks, change daily fluctuations, and alter the timing and volume of downstream discharge. Dams, diversions, poorly designed road-stream crossings, levees and channelization can impede aquatic passage, disconnect floodplains or stream reaches, and alter the timing, magnitude, velocity or local distribution of river flow.

Constriction, perched outlets, and crossing geometry can change local velocity, depth, sediment transport, and channel form relative to an unimpeded reference reach. Dams, diversions, poorly designed road-stream crossings, levees and channelization can impede aquatic passage, disconnect floodplains or stream reaches, and alter the timing, magnitude, velocity or local distribution of river flow.

Confinement and straightening can accelerate downstream transport, change water depth and velocity, alter inundation frequency, and separate the main channel from floodplain storage. Dams, diversions, poorly designed road-stream crossings, levees and channelization can impede aquatic passage, disconnect floodplains or stream reaches, and alter the timing, magnitude, velocity or local distribution of river flow.

Sustained heavy precipitation can raise runoff and streamflow sharply, especially when soils are saturated, snow melts, or terrain focuses rainfall into a river network. Many detected events replenish water supplies without damaging flow, while dry soils, storage, weak lift, or short duration can limit runoff.
outgoing: When river discharge weakens or shifts seasonally, freshwater resistance to estuarine salinity intrusion drops and inland salt fronts can move farther upstream. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of river flow regime change.

River flow regime shift destabilizes reservoir storage instability when inflow timing and volume depart from operating assumptions. Reservoirs may then refill at the wrong time or fail to hold enough water for dry-season demand.

River flow regime shift pressures basin treaty breakdown when historical allocation rules no longer match available flow. Allocation rules based on historical flows can become harder to honor, increasing conflict between upstream and downstream users.

River flow regime shift creates reservoir operating shortfall when release rules cannot match altered inflow timing. Operators may then miss flood-control, hydropower, water-supply, or environmental-flow targets.

Hydropower reliability falls when river timing and seasonal flow patterns no longer match reservoir and turbine expectations. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of river flow regime change.

reservoir storage instability.name: Reservoir Storage Instability
reservoir storage instability.description: Greater variability and reduced reliability in reservoir storage. Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support.
incoming: River flow regime shift destabilizes reservoir storage instability when inflow timing and volume depart from operating assumptions. Reservoirs may then refill at the wrong time or fail to hold enough water for dry-season demand.
Through prolonged inflow deficits, Drought Persistence deepens Reservoir Storage Instability. As inflows remain low, reservoirs may not refill enough to meet water, power, and ecological needs.

Through diminished seasonal snowpack storage, Snow Drought raises Reservoir Storage Instability. Reservoirs may refill earlier but still enter summer with less stored water for farms, cities, and ecosystems.

Suspended and bed material settles as flow velocity declines in impoundments, progressively occupying storage and affecting intakes where loads are sustained. How strongly this effect develops depends on reservoir geometry, flushing operations, and grain size.
outgoing: Reservoir-storage instability becomes operationally visible when managers can no longer count on expected usable storage, release timing, or generation support. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of reservoir storage instability.

shift in snowmelt timing.name: Shift in Snowmelt Timing
shift in snowmelt timing.description: A shift in when seasonal snow begins melting and when its runoff reaches downstream rivers and reservoirs. Earlier or faster snowmelt increases liquid water within the mountain snowpack and weakens its internal structure.
incoming: Darkening snow with black carbon lowers reflectivity and can accelerate earlier melt, making this a local frozen-water system process. Advances by lowering snow surface reflectivity and accelerating melt.

Warmer air causes snow to melt earlier, shifting the spring runoff peak and changing when rivers receive water from the seasonal snowpack. Across 2,339 snow-affected, minimally impaired Northern Hemisphere catchments, a 1 degree Celsius increase in catchment annual mean air temperature was associated on average with a 4.7-day advance in the annual maximum snowmelt-flood peak date, with a 5.0-day cross-catchment standard deviation.

A smaller or warmer seasonal snowpack often melts earlier and produces a weaker spring pulse, shifting the timing of runoff. Snow drought can condition snowmelt timing shift through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.

Carbon-dioxide emissions warm snow-dominated basins, causing winter precipitation to fall more often as rain and advancing the seasonal timing of snowmelt. Cumulative greenhouse-gas emissions alter heat trapped in the climate system and climate, which can change snow accumulation and melt timing, drought and heavy-precipitation conditions, flood-generating processes, water quality and freshwater ecosystems.

Dark mineral particles reduce snow surface reflectivity, increase shortwave-energy absorption, accelerate grain growth and melt, and expose darker ground earlier, shifting melt and peak runoff toward earlier dates. Fresh snowfall can temporarily bury dust, cloud cover reduces shortwave forcing, and the magnitude cannot be transferred between basins without local snow-energy modeling.
outgoing: Earlier or faster snowmelt can shift runoff timing and intensify melt-season flow pulses, especially where storage is limited. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of shift in snowmelt timing increases.

Snowmelt timing shift advances river flow regime shift by moving runoff away from historical seasonal timing. Earlier snowmelt can shift snow-fed river flow toward earlier seasonal runoff and reduce warm-season contribution where storage and rainfall do not compensate.

Earlier or faster snowmelt increases liquid water within the mountain snowpack and weakens its internal structure. Wet-snow avalanche risk can rise when saturated layers lose cohesion above exposed passes.
Earlier snowmelt delivers water to glacier drainage systems sooner and can raise pressure before channels are fully developed. Rapid reorganization or blockage can release stored water as a flood.

Earlier snowmelt changes the seasonal timing and apparent composition of mountain runoff, helping expose when former glacier-melt buffering no longer sustains late-season flow. Some glacier-fed basins are moving past the stage of rising meltwater supply and into long-term decline, changing the reliability of downstream seasonal water systems.

Earlier loss of seasonal snow can reduce the duration and extent of cool, moist snowbed microhabitat on alpine or polar nunataks, exposing specialised biota to longer growing-season heat and desiccation. Named nunatak or alpine snowbed with snow disappearance date, soil moisture and temperature, mapped microhabitat and species occupancy measured together.

flash flood regime.name: Flash Flood Regime
flash flood regime.description: The recurring pattern, timing, and severity of fast-rising floods after intense rain or sudden water release. Standing water, damaged drainage, altered water storage, and service disruption can increase mosquito breeding and human-vector contact.
incoming: Heavier short-duration rainfall increases flash-flood risk when rainfall rates overwhelm local drainage, infiltration, and channel capacity. More intense short-duration precipitation can increase the frequency or magnitude of pluvial and flash flooding when rainfall rates exceed local infiltration, channel, storage or artificial-drainage capacity.

Greater atmospheric moisture can intensify short-duration rainfall, but flash flooding also depends on storm dynamics, terrain, drainage, and antecedent conditions. Greater atmospheric moisture can raise short-duration extreme-rainfall potential and thereby increase flash-flood hazard when storms, terrain, soils, drainage and antecedent wetness convert rainfall into rapid runoff.

Active Madden-Julian Oscillation convection can raise heavy-rainfall and flash-flood potential, conditional on regional moisture and terrain. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of madden-julian oscillation.

A warmer atmosphere can intensify short-duration rainfall extremes, making temperature an upstream driver of flash-flood regime change. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Carbon Emission intensifies heavy rainfall and can increase flash-flood risk where terrain, soil, and drainage conditions permit. Cumulative greenhouse-gas emissions alter heat trapped in the climate system and climate, which can change snow accumulation and melt timing, drought and heavy-precipitation conditions, flood-generating processes, water quality and freshwater ecosystems.
outgoing: Short-duration flood pulses can exceed sewer and treatment capacity, making flash-flood regime change an upstream driver of overflow risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of flash flood regime.

Through turbidity, contamination, and intake disruption, Flash Flood Regime overloads Drinking Water Treatment Stress. Treatment plants may need to slow intake or add filtration and disinfection while contamination remains elevated.

Standing water, damaged drainage, altered water storage, and service disruption can increase mosquito breeding and human-vector contact. Flooding and associated water and sanitation disruption can create breeding habitat and increase exposure for some vector-borne diseases.

Floodwater can contaminate drinking-water facilities and increase exposure to water-borne pathogens where treatment and hygiene controls fail. Magnitude and timing require a named regional observation.

drought persistence.name: Drought Persistence
drought persistence.description: Monitors multi-season drought persistence and carryover effects in soil and reservoirs.
incoming: Persistent blocking suppresses storm passage and precipitation beneath the block, sustaining regional drought conditions. Persistent blocking can prolong regional drought by repeatedly diverting storm tracks and suppressing precipitation over the blocked region.

Persistent North Atlantic Oscillation phases can sustain regional precipitation deficits, but drought outcomes depend on season and location. Modulates through regional precipitation and storm-track anomalies.
The Pacific-North American pattern can steer rain away from a region for a season, helping drought persist. The result depends on the pattern phase and time of year.

Slow planetary-wave patterns can sustain rainfall suppression and drought, but attribution varies by event. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of persistent rossby wave patterns.
Warmer air pulls more water from soil and plants. Where rain does not replace that loss, drought can become more severe and last longer.

Arctic Oscillation phases alter pressure, storm-track and temperature patterns. In some regions and seasons, the resulting precipitation deficits, early warming, snowmelt and water loss from soil and plants can contribute to persistent dryness into the following season.

El Niño reorganizes tropical convection and atmospheric circulation, producing sustained rainfall deficits in some regions. Weather deficits can persist through soil-moisture, river-flow, reservoir and peatland memory after the atmospheric anomaly develops, extending agricultural, water-related and fire-weather drought conditions.

Carbon-dioxide emissions warm land and increase atmospheric demand for moisture. Where precipitation remains deficient, faster drying can deepen soil and vegetation stress and allow drought conditions to persist.
Compound climate hazards can include persistent agricultural and ecological drought in drying regions. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
outgoing: Prolonged drought reduces river flow and estuarine flushing, allowing saline fronts to penetrate farther inland and persist longer. Extends when prolonged low-flow conditions allow saline fronts to move farther inland.
Through prolonged inflow deficits, Drought Persistence deepens Reservoir Storage Instability. As inflows remain low, reservoirs may not refill enough to meet water, power, and ecological needs.

Persistent precipitation deficit and evaporative demand can drive soil moisture to exceptionally low levels when storage is not replenished. Research supports this direct process: drought_persistence drives soil_moisture_collapse when root-zone moisture cannot recover seasonally.

Drought persistence raises pressure on basin treaty breakdown through repeated cross-border allocation shortfalls. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of drought persistence increases.

Drought persistence intensifies drinking water treatment stress through lower source volume and concentrated contaminants. Utilities may need more intensive treatment as pollutants and salts become concentrated in smaller water volumes.
Drought persistence increases risk of hydropower reliability decline through sustained inflow and head deficits. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of drought persistence.

Drought persistence raises risk of peat oxidation pulse through peat drying and oxygen exposure. Peat oxidation is treated as a carbon-cycle feedback because the United States space agency Earthdata maintains peatland data access and monitoring processes relevant to peat carbon storage, drainage, fire, and release risk.

Persistent drought dries soils and reduces evaporative cooling, leaving crops, livestock and farm workers exposed to hotter local conditions. Drought persistence can condition farm heat stress through the reviewed food mechanism.

Persistent drought dries live and dead vegetation across seasons, increasing the amount of burnable fuel and lengthening the period of elevated fire risk. Drought persistence can condition wildfire regime shift through the reviewed extremes mechanism.

Persistent drought reduces aquifer recharge while often increasing pumping demand, accelerating groundwater depletion where withdrawals already approach sustainable limits. Aquifers are being drawn down faster than they recharge, turning hidden water reserves into a long-lived constraint on farming, drinking water, and ecosystem resilience.

Persistent drought reduces surface supply and groundwater recharge, increasing water stress when demand remains high. Persistent imbalance between water demand and available supply raises the baseline fragility of cities, farms, power systems, and river ecosystems.

Persistent drought reduces soil moisture and water loss from soil and plants, increasing sensible heating and atmospheric demand for water. Drought persistence can condition atmospheric dryness through the reviewed extremes mechanism.

Persistent precipitation deficits reduce water available to cross the soil and unsaturated zone into an aquifer, with groundwater response often delayed. Groundwater levels can fall during drought because of increased pumping even where recharge change is poorly constrained.

Persistent or repeated drought depletes plant moisture reserves, raises mortality and fire susceptibility, and can shift survival of young animals into adulthood and competitive balance toward drier vegetation. A single drought can cause mortality without creating a persistent biome transition, and forest resilience varies regionally.
Repeated moisture deficits reduce plant cover and recovery, leaving soil more exposed to wind and water erosion. The effect becomes stronger where management has already lowered resilience.

Repeated moisture deficits can dry the surface and suppress plant cover, increasing the availability of loose sediment when strong winds occur. Drought alone does not create a storm and may not increase emissions where soil crusts, vegetation, or weak winds limit erosion.
Mountain Forest Cover and Treeline Contraction

Persistent moisture shortage reduces plant-available water and growth, increases hydraulic and carbon stress, weakens seedlings and mature trees, and can leave disturbed areas unable to return to their prior forest state. Some forests recover after drought, thinning can reduce competition, cooler or wetter high elevations may retain sufficient moisture, and a short greenness decline is not persistent cover loss.

Repeated moisture deficit can suppress woody survival of young animals into adulthood and survival where rainfall and soils already constrain tree establishment. Named savanna with fixed woody-cover observations and climate history.

Sustained water deficit can impair hydraulic transport and carbon balance, increasing death risk directly and through weakened defenses. Persistent water limitation can increase overstory tree mortality risk through hydraulic stress and atmospheric moisture demand, but temperature alone is not an adequate exposure proxy and vapor-pressure deficit can dominate the response.

Prolonged low flow can expose beds, raise temperature, reduce oxygen, concentrate contaminants, and interrupt host-fish access. Named river reach and mussel bed with flow, temperature, water quality and survival observations.

Severe water stress can reduce resin production and other tree defences, allowing sufficiently abundant aggressive beetles to overcome hosts more successfully. The response is non-linear: moderate drought can reduce beetle performance, and evidence is weak for a drought role in some species such as southern pine beetle.

Sustained moisture deficits can impair hydraulic function and tree survival, especially where heat, pests, fire injury, or stand condition add stress. Magnitude and timing require a named regional observation.

Prolonged drying can degrade vegetation cover, soil condition, and fertility, placing soil biological communities and their functions under stress. Magnitude and timing require a named regional observation.

Persistent precipitation deficits and reduced inflow can lower or destabilize reservoir, lake, and river storage where withdrawals continue. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.

Extended drought can reduce urban source-water availability and prompt restrictions, moderated by storage, transfers, leakage, pricing, and conservation. Use only within the geography, system boundary, and exposure conditions stated by the cited evidence.

Prolonged precipitation and runoff deficits reduce river and reservoir inflows, with snow storage and groundwater buffering moderating timing. Documented precipitation, streamflow, or runoff deficit to a named surface-water body.

Extended drought can reduce reservoir inflow, river yield, and groundwater recharge available to urban systems. Measured shortfall in a utility’s surface-water, reservoir, or groundwater supply relative to demand and operating rules.

freshwater lens thinning in small island.name: Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands
freshwater lens thinning in small island.description: The thinning of the floating freshwater reserve beneath a small island as pumping, drought, or saltwater intrusion reduces its usable depth. When thin freshwater lenses can no longer supply reliable potable water, communities often become more dependent on desalination or imported water.
incoming: Rising sea level can thin and salinize shallow freshwater lenses on small islands by increasing saltwater intrusion pressure from below and the coast. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of sea-level rise increases.

Overpumping lowers freshwater heads and makes small-island lenses more vulnerable to saltwater intrusion and usable-storage loss. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of aquifer overdraft.

Advancing saline fronts and tidal pressure can intensify intrusion into shallow coastal freshwater bodies, thinning already vulnerable freshwater lenses. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of delta salt intrusion fronts increases.
Carbon Emission contributes to sea-level rise and coastal flooding pressures that can compress freshwater lenses on low islands. Downstream attribution is indirect unless stated otherwise.
outgoing: Through salinity and reduced potable-water availability, Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands increases Drinking Water Treatment Stress. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of freshwater lens thinning in small islands.

drinking water treatment stress.name: Drinking Water Treatment Stress
drinking water treatment stress.description: Pressure on drinking water treatment severe enough to impair normal function or recovery. Persistent treatment stress from salinity and source-water degradation can harden into a shift toward desalination where utilities need a more salt-tolerant supply option.
incoming: Bypass discharge can raise contaminant and turbidity loads in receiving waters, increasing treatment difficulty and cost for downstream utilities. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of wastewater bypass discharge.

Forest loss in source watersheds can raise erosion, turbidity, and runoff volatility, increasing treatment strain for downstream drinking-water systems. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of watershed forest loss increases.

Salt intrusion can threaten freshwater intakes and raise treatment difficulty, forcing utilities to manage salinity spikes, blending limits, and intake shifts. Threatens when saline water intrudes into source intakes and treatment systems.

Through salinity and reduced potable-water availability, Freshwater Lens Thinning in Small Islands increases Drinking Water Treatment Stress. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of freshwater lens thinning in small islands.

As coastal groundwater becomes more saline or degraded, utilities and users lose raw-water flexibility and face higher treatment and substitution burdens. Coastal Aquifer Salinization raises when salinized groundwater reduces raw-water quality and supply flexibility.

Coastal flooding and saline inundation can degrade raw-water quality, impair intake operations, and raise treatment stress for exposed drinking-water systems. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of coastal inundation risk.

Through turbidity, contamination, and intake disruption, Flash Flood Regime overloads Drinking Water Treatment Stress. Treatment plants may need to slow intake or add filtration and disinfection while contamination remains elevated.

Drought persistence intensifies drinking water treatment stress through lower source volume and concentrated contaminants. Utilities may need more intensive treatment as pollutants and salts become concentrated in smaller water volumes.

watershed forest loss.name: Watershed Forest Loss
watershed forest loss.description: The removal or death of forest cover within a drainage basin. Loss of watershed and bank vegetation can increase runoff and sediment delivery while reducing root reinforcement at exposed banks.
incoming: Warming and drying pressure raise watershed forest stress by increasing fire exposure, water loss from soil and plants pressure, and hydrologic instability across forested basins. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Clearing forest within a watershed removes canopy and root structure, reducing forest cover while increasing erosion and rapid runoff into streams. Deforestation can condition watershed forest loss through the reviewed biodiversity mechanism.

Repeated severe fires can convert forested watersheds to lower-cover vegetation when tree mortality outpaces regeneration. Wildfire regime shift can condition watershed forest loss through the reviewed biodiversity mechanism.
outgoing: Loss of forest cover in key watersheds can degrade stream habitat, sediment conditions, and ecological buffering, pushing freshwater ecosystems toward collapse. Degrades toward through erosion and runoff change.

Forest loss in source watersheds can raise erosion, turbidity, and runoff volatility, increasing treatment strain for downstream drinking-water systems. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of watershed forest loss increases.

Watershed forest degradation can destabilize runoff timing and sediment conditions that matter for dependable hydropower operations. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of watershed forest loss.

Watershed forest loss intensifies riverine habitat fragmentation through erosion, channel alteration, and riparian loss. Sediment, warmer water, and damaged streambanks can isolate habitat and disrupt fish movement.

Loss of watershed and bank vegetation can increase runoff and sediment delivery while reducing root reinforcement at exposed banks. Named harvested or cleared catchment and riparian reach with land-cover and bank observations.

wastewater infrastructure overflow.name: Wastewater Infrastructure Overflow
wastewater infrastructure overflow.description: Wastewater escaping from sewers, pumps, treatment plants, or storage after their capacity is exceeded. Loss of safe water and sanitation controls can expose people to pathogen-contaminated water and raise outbreak risk after flooding or system failure.
incoming: Short-duration flood pulses can exceed sewer and treatment capacity, making flash-flood regime change an upstream driver of overflow risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of flash flood regime.

Higher baseline coastal water levels can impair drainage and push wastewater systems toward backup and overflow during storms or high tides. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal inundation risk.

More intense short-duration precipitation can exceed sewer conveyance and treatment-system design capacity, increasing overflow risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of extreme precipitation intensity.

Flood-Resilient Infrastructure reduces Wastewater Infrastructure Overflow through separated flows, added capacity, storage, and floodproofing. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.
outgoing: Overflow conditions often manifest operationally as bypass or emergency discharge events when plants and sewers exceed safe handling limits. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of wastewater infrastructure overflow.

When a combined wastewater system is hydraulically overloaded, discharge from its designated outfall is a combined sewer overflow. Applies only where a combined sewer system and a documented overflow process exist.

wastewater bypass discharge.name: Wastewater Bypass Discharge
wastewater bypass discharge.description: Untreated or partly treated wastewater released around a normal treatment step during overload, failure, or maintenance. Untreated or bypassed wastewater delivers nitrogen and phosphorus to receiving waters.
incoming: Overflow conditions often manifest operationally as bypass or emergency discharge events when plants and sewers exceed safe handling limits. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of wastewater infrastructure overflow.

Water Reuse and Recycling can reduce Wastewater Bypass Discharge when reuse investment also improves collection and treatment. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.
outgoing: Bypass discharge can raise contaminant and turbidity loads in receiving waters, increasing treatment difficulty and cost for downstream utilities. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of wastewater bypass discharge.

Nutrient-rich bypass discharge can help trigger harmful algal blooms where warm temperatures, low flushing, and bloom-prone waters already exist. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of wastewater bypass discharge.

Organic and nutrient loads from untreated or partially treated wastewater can increase oxygen demand and contribute to estuarine and nearshore hypoxia. Wastewater Bypass Discharge contributes to through oxygen-demanding organic and nutrient loads in estuaries and nearshore waters.

Wastewater bypass discharge contributes to freshwater ecosystem collapse through pathogen, nutrient, and contaminant loading. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of wastewater bypass discharge.
Untreated or bypassed wastewater delivers nitrogen and phosphorus to receiving waters. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus loading that degrades fresh and coastal waters.

Untreated or partially treated discharges can deliver nitrogen, phosphorus, and oxygen-demanding organic matter directly to receiving waters, increasing enrichment and respiration pressure. The relationship is limited to the stated mechanism, geography, time, and measurement boundary.

Sewage and related contaminants from wastewater bypass discharge reduce water and sediment quality, impairing kelp growth and reproduction in exposed nearshore habitat. Repeated or sustained exposure can shrink canopy area and prevent recovery, contributing to kelp forest collapse when plume transport, concentration, duration and biological observations confirm contact.

irrigation water inefficiency.name: Irrigation Water Inefficiency
irrigation water inefficiency.description: The loss of irrigation water before it benefits crops through evaporation, leakage, runoff, or poorly matched application. Inefficient irrigation requires more pumping for each unit of crop production, depleting aquifers when the additional withdrawal is not returned as usable recharge.
incoming: Industry farming can embed irrigation water inefficiency through poorly matched application and conveyance losses. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of industry farming.
outgoing: Irrigation water inefficiency intensifies aquifer overdraft when avoidable losses are replaced through pumping. Low irrigation application or conveyance efficiency can increase gross groundwater withdrawals and contribute to aquifer overdraft where pumping persistently exceeds recharge and return flows.

Irrigation water inefficiency deepens groundwater depletion wells through higher withdrawals per unit of crop output. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of irrigation water inefficiency.

Inefficient irrigation requires more pumping for each unit of crop production, depleting aquifers when the additional withdrawal is not returned as usable recharge. Aquifers are being drawn down faster than they recharge, turning hidden water reserves into a long-lived constraint on farming, drinking water, and ecosystem resilience.

Inadequate irrigation and drainage management can leave dissolved salts in the root zone or raise saline groundwater, progressively salinizing agricultural soil. Irrigated fields with insufficient leaching or drainage and measured water-quality context.

incoming: Operating shortfalls are a direct process into hydropower reliability decline because constrained storage and release flexibility reduce dependable generation. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of reservoir operating shortfall.

Drought persistence increases risk of hydropower reliability decline through sustained inflow and head deficits. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of drought persistence.

Glacier meltwater dependency raises risk for hydropower reliability decline through altered seasonal water supply. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of glacier-fed water dependence.

Hydropower reliability falls when river timing and seasonal flow patterns no longer match reservoir and turbine expectations. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of river flow regime change.

Fresh meltwater from Greenland lowers North Atlantic surface salinity and density, making deep-water formation less efficient and potentially weakening Atlantic overturning. sea ice season loss.name: Sea Ice Season Loss
sea ice season loss.description: A shortening of the part of the year when a region remains covered by sea ice. A longer ice-free season can extend Arctic navigation windows, although mobile ice, severe weather, port access, insurance and regulation still determine whether shipping expands.
incoming: Higher global temperatures melt Arctic sea ice earlier and delay its return in autumn, shortening the annual sea-ice season. At stabilized global warming of 2 degrees Celsius, the assessed annual probability of a practically sea-ice-free Arctic September by the end of the century is 10-35 percent, compared with approximately 1 percent at 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Ocean heat melts sea ice from below and delays autumn freeze-up, shortening the period of seasonal ice cover. Ocean heat content can condition sea ice season loss through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.

Rapid Arctic warming accelerates spring melt and delays autumn freeze-up, shortening the annual sea-ice season. Arctic amplification rates can condition sea ice season loss through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.
Carbon dioxide emissions warm the Arctic, causing sea ice to melt earlier and form later. This shortens the season when the ocean remains ice-covered.
outgoing: A longer ice-free season can extend Arctic navigation windows, although mobile ice, severe weather, port access, insurance and regulation still determine whether shipping expands. Sea ice season loss can condition arctic shipping expansion through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.
Loss of reflective sea ice increases absorbed solar energy and contributes to amplified Arctic warming. Sea Ice Season Loss amplifies warming through via lower surface reflectivity.

Sea ice season loss raises exposure to polar infrastructure failure through coastal erosion, waves, and shorter stable access seasons. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of sea ice season loss.
A shorter sea-ice season leaves a thinner, less consolidated Arctic ice cover. Wind and currents can move that mobile pack more quickly and unpredictably across navigation areas.

A shorter sea-ice season reduces the stable habitat available for ice algae and changes when light reaches them. Earlier melt can shift bloom timing and reduce pigment biomass retained within the ice.

A longer open-water season increases fetch and the duration of wave attack on vulnerable Arctic coastlines, amplifying thermal and mechanical erosion of thawing bluffs. Arctic coasts underlain by thawing permafrost can erode rapidly as warmer ground, sea-ice loss, and wave attack destabilize bluffs, roads, settlements, and shore infrastructure.

Seasonal sea-ice loss replaces high-surface reflectivity ice with dark ocean during the sunlit season, increasing absorbed shortwave energy and strengthening the ice-surface reflectivity feedback. Thaw weakens ice-rich Arctic coastal ground and increases susceptibility to erosion, while seasonal sea-ice loss exposes darker ocean that absorbs more solar energy and contributes to the positive surface reflectivity feedback and amplified Arctic warming.

coastal inundation risk.name: Coastal Inundation Risk
coastal inundation risk.description: The likelihood or potential severity of coastal inundation. Storm surge, astronomical tide and sea-level rise combine to inundate low-elevation coastal assets.
incoming: Nature-Based Adaptation can reduce exposure to Coastal Inundation Risk through mangroves, marshes, dunes, and reefs within their physical limits. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Higher global temperature raises sea level by expanding ocean water and accelerating land-ice melt, making warming a direct upstream driver of coastal inundation risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Carbon emissions load the climate system with warming that contributes to sea-level rise, strengthening the baseline flood and erosion risk facing coasts. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of carbon emission increases.

Atlantic overturning circulation variability can alter regional dynamic sea level along parts of the North Atlantic coast, changing inundation risk without determining global coastal outcomes. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of atlantic overturning circulation slowdown increases.

Earth rotation and current momentum maintain a sea-surface-height gradient across the Florida Straits. Weaker flow reduces that gradient and is associated with higher water levels along the nearby Atlantic coast.
Ice-sheet-driven sea-level rise increases coastal inundation risk where exposure, tides, storms, and local land motion align. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.

Rising regional mean sea level elevates the baseline coastal water level, causing historically rare extreme still-water levels to be exceeded more frequently where tides, surge, waves, vertical land motion, and exposure align. Regional relative sea-level rise is assessed to amplify the occurrence frequency of recent-past extreme still-water levels by roughly 20-30 times by 2050 across quasi-global tide-gauge locations.
outgoing: Higher baseline coastal water levels can impair drainage and push wastewater systems toward backup and overflow during storms or high tides. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal inundation risk.

Higher coastal water levels allow saline water to penetrate farther inland through estuaries, deltas, and connected coastal aquifers, especially during low-flow periods. Salt fronts can push farther inland in deltas and estuaries as sea level rises, river discharge weakens, and storm-driven water levels press saline water into farms and intakes.

Repeated coastal flooding and higher saline water tables can degrade connected coastal groundwater, especially where aquifers are shallow and hydraulically exposed. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal inundation risk.

Coastal flooding and saline inundation can degrade raw-water quality, impair intake operations, and raise treatment stress for exposed drinking-water systems. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of coastal inundation risk.
Coastal Inundation Risk raises Airport Climate Exposure for low-lying coastal airports. Flooded runways and access roads can delay flights, damage equipment, and interrupt regional transport.

Coastal inundation risk increases pressure for coastal property insurance redlines through repeated flood loss and repricing. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal inundation risk.

Coastal inundation risk raises risk of tidal wetland carbon reversal where wetlands cannot migrate or accrete fast enough. Tidal wetland carbon reversal is modelled as a distinct coastal carbon feedback using the United States ocean and atmosphere agency blue-carbon program material on carbon storage in salt marsh, mangrove, and seagrass systems and the risk of reversal under disturbance and loss.

Coastal Inundation Risk increases the need for Flood-Resilient Infrastructure where essential services face recurring coastal flooding. This is a reviewed system-response process supported by the attached sector assessment, not a claim of a universal project-level effect.

Storm surge, astronomical tide and sea-level rise combine to inundate low-elevation coastal assets. Water depth and extent intersected with infrastructure and building inventories create direct physical exposure and damage potential.

Repeated coastal flooding raises expected claims and reinsurance costs, encouraging insurers to increase prices, restrict coverage or leave exposed markets. Documents insurance premium increases, carrier withdrawals, and nonrenewals in climate-exposed housing markets.

Coastal flooding can close ports, damage access roads and interrupt cargo handling, disrupting shipping even when offshore lanes remain open. Coastal inundation risk can condition shipping lane disruption through the reviewed infrastructure mechanism.

Sea-level-driven salinity changes can alter estuarine habitat suitability for pathogens with bounded salinity optima, changing exposure risk in particular estuaries. Warmer water and changing coastal conditions expand the range or seasonality of marine pathogens that threaten shellfish safety, fisheries, and coastal health systems.

Sea-water intrusion and saline flooding can deliver salts to low-lying agricultural soils and freshwater sources, increasing root-zone salinity risk. How strongly this effect develops depends on elevation, storm frequency, and drainage.

Repeated or projected coastal inundation can make continued protection, rebuilding, or accommodation infeasible, increasing the need to evaluate rights-based managed retreat or planned relocation. Named coastal settlement or asset class with mapped inundation, exposure, protection standard, residual risk, tenure, and relocation options.

polar infrastructure failure.name: Polar Infrastructure Failure
polar infrastructure failure.description: The point at which polar infrastructure can no longer perform its expected function. Failures in remote polar assets, transport links, and utility structures are a concrete local form of broader infrastructure fragility.
incoming: Thermokarst-driven subsidence and ponding are a direct operational hazard for roads, pads, pipelines, and foundations in thawing high-latitude terrain. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of thermokarst expansion.

Sea ice season loss raises exposure to polar infrastructure failure through coastal erosion, waves, and shorter stable access seasons. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of sea ice season loss.

Warming increases active-layer thickness and can thaw excess ground ice. The resulting loss of ground volume, differential settlement, subsidence, drainage change and slope instability can reduce foundation bearing capacity, distort embankments and disrupt transport or utility assets built on susceptible permafrost.

Rapid shoreline retreat and bluff failure can undermine roads, buildings, utilities, and access infrastructure located on or near unstable Arctic coasts. Settlements and facilities on eroding Arctic permafrost coasts.
Carbon Emission contributes to permafrost thaw, sea-ice loss, and extreme conditions that threaten polar infrastructure. Downstream attribution is indirect unless stated otherwise.
Ice loss and associated coastal and permafrost change can raise polar infrastructure risk where assets depend on stable ice or ground. Interpret through named regional or local conditions.
outgoing: Failures in remote polar assets, transport links, and utility structures are a concrete local form of broader infrastructure fragility. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of polar infrastructure failure.

snow drought.name: Snow Drought
snow drought.description: An unusually small snowpack, or an early loss of stored snow, that reduces dependable cold-season water storage. A smaller or warmer seasonal snowpack often melts earlier and produces a weaker spring pulse, shifting the timing of runoff.
incoming: Warming shifts precipitation phase and accelerates snow loss, making higher temperature an upstream driver of snow-drought risk. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of warming.

Carbon-dioxide-driven warming causes more winter precipitation to fall as rain and accelerates melt from the snowpack. Mountain basins can enter snow drought when seasonal snow-water storage falls well below its expected level.
outgoing: Through reduced and earlier snowmelt runoff, Snow Drought intensifies River Flow Regime Change. Rivers then receive a smaller, earlier spring pulse and less water during the warm season.

Through diminished seasonal snowpack storage, Snow Drought raises Reservoir Storage Instability. Reservoirs may refill earlier but still enter summer with less stored water for farms, cities, and ecosystems.

A smaller or warmer seasonal snowpack often melts earlier and produces a weaker spring pulse, shifting the timing of runoff. Snow drought can condition snowmelt timing shift through the reviewed frozen-water system mechanism.

Reduced snow accumulation decreases seasonal storage and can make basins more dependent on a shrinking glacier contribution, increasing post-peak late-season supply risk. Some glacier-fed basins are moving past the stage of rising meltwater supply and into long-term decline, changing the reliability of downstream seasonal water systems.

A snow drought leaves mountain snowpacks smaller because less snow falls, more rain falls instead, or warm weather melts the snow early. A snow-drought season reduces seasonal snow water storage through low snowfall, rain-on-snow conditions, or warm-season melt anomalies.

Persistent snow-accumulation deficits reduce mass input to small ice caps. Where ablation remains high, negative surface mass balance can thin summit and connecting ice until formerly continuous cap geometry fragments.

oceanic deoxygenation.name: Oceanic Deoxygenation
oceanic deoxygenation.description: Declining dissolved oxygen across the open ocean and deep waters compresses habitable space and weakens marine ecosystem resilience.
incoming: Ocean warming lowers the amount of oxygen water can hold and strengthens ocean layering and reduces ventilation that drive deoxygenation. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of warming increases.

Layering that limits mixing restricts vertical ventilation and oxygen renewal in subsurface waters. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of ocean salinity layering that limits mixing increases.

Weaker abyssal overturning reduces ventilation and renewal of oxygenated deep water. In the Australian Antarctic Basin over 1994-2017, reduced Antarctic Bottom Water transport and contraction of the well-ventilated layer were associated with a basin-mean contraction-driven dissolved-oxygen decline of 3 plus or minus 2 micromoles per kilogram per decade.

Carbon-dioxide-driven warming reduces the amount of oxygen water can hold and strengthens ocean layering that limits mixing, limiting ventilation of deeper water. Those changes contribute to long-term oxygen decline across open-ocean and abyssal layers.
outgoing: Low oxygen compresses viable habitat and excludes oxygen-sensitive organisms, reorganizing marine communities. Persistent low oxygen can exclude or kill oxygen-sensitive organisms and favour tolerant taxa, simplifying local marine food-web structure when exposure exceeds species thresholds.

Deoxygenation contributes to fishery risk through habitat compression, mortality, and stock redistribution. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of oceanic deoxygenation.

Declining oxygen in source waters lowers the background concentration entering a shelf system, reducing the additional oxygen consumption needed to cross a local hypoxia threshold. The relationship is limited to the stated mechanism, geography, time, and measurement boundary.

Declining dissolved oxygen can narrow habitable depth and temperature space, change prey fields, and force mobile organisms toward regions or layers with adequate oxygen. Tolerance and behavioral response differ strongly by species, and local oxygen changes can be driven by nutrient pollution rather than global climate forcing.

outgoing: Lower carbonate-ion concentration and saturation state make it harder for calcifying shellfish to build and maintain calcium-carbonate shells. Lower aragonite saturation can reduce coral calcification, with a meta-analytic mean response of about 15 percent per unit decrease in aragonite saturation within the studied range, but responses vary substantially across studies, taxa and methods.
More acidic ocean water stresses sensitive species and changes who eats whom. These disruptions can simplify the food web and reduce energy available to larger animals.

Ocean acidification contributes to reef structural collapse through calcification stress and slower framework recovery. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of ocean acidification increases.

Lower carbonate saturation and pH can reduce survival, growth, development, or habitat-finding in sensitive larvae and shell-forming species, weakening nursery function where exposure is sustained. Responses differ across taxa and life stages, and exposure alone does not establish loss of whole-estuary nursery function without survival of young animals into adulthood or habitat evidence.

Acidification reduces coral growth and resilience, making reefs less able to tolerate and recover from thermal bleaching stress rather than serving as a standalone bleaching measure. This process is reef-specific and does not assume a uniform bleaching response across coral taxa or locations.

Reduced calcification and enhanced framework erosion can make structures more fragile, increasing susceptibility to breakage when waves or other disturbances occur. Calcifying reefs with measured carbonate chemistry, accretion or erosion, and structural condition.
Changing carbonate chemistry can affect growth, reproduction, sensory performance, calcifying prey, and habitat. These effects may alter realized ranges when combined with warming and oxygen loss.

pacific decadal oscillation.name: Pacific Decadal Oscillation
pacific decadal oscillation.description: A long-lived pattern of North Pacific temperature variability shifts regional rainfall, marine conditions, and background climate over years to decades.
incoming: El Niño can leave a multi-year imprint on North Pacific temperature and circulation, contributing to Pacific Decadal Oscillation variability alongside internal ocean dynamics. El nino can condition pacific decadal oscillation through the reviewed climate dynamics mechanism.

outgoing: The phase of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation can make ocean heatwaves in the northeast Pacific more or less frequent, long-lasting, and intense. Observed Pacific Decadal Oscillation phase modulates Northeast Pacific marine-heatwave frequency, duration, and intensity.

The Pacific Decadal Oscillation shifts ocean temperatures and weather patterns across the North Pacific and nearby continents over many years. Pacific Decadal Oscillation is a monitored natural mode that organizes regional sea-surface temperature and climate anomalies.

Pacific Decadal Oscillation changes linked to the Pacific Decadal Oscillation can make parts of the ocean more or less suitable for a species, causing fish and other open-ocean animals to move. Pacific Decadal Oscillation-linked habitat anomalies can shift species availability and distribution.

North Pacific temperature patterns associated with the Pacific Decadal Oscillation can alter atmospheric wave propagation and the likelihood of particular Pacific-North American pattern phases. Pacific decadal oscillation can condition pacific north american pattern through the reviewed climate dynamics mechanism.

Persistent North Pacific sea-surface-temperature patterns can alter atmospheric wave trains and condition jet-stream position and variability over the Pacific-North American sector. These are bounded conditioning mechanisms, not deterministic trend claims.

marine fisheries collapse.name: Marine Fisheries Collapse
marine fisheries collapse.description: A severe loss of fish abundance or reproductive capacity that prevents a fishery from sustaining normal harvest and ecosystem roles. A sustained decline in accessible stock can reduce expected catch and revenue, intensifying competition among fleets or states where access is contested and institutions cannot adjust allocation peacefully.
incoming: When estuary nursery habitat declines, fewer young fish and shellfish survive to replenish coastal fisheries. Stocks can then become more vulnerable to collapse.

Marine heatwaves can cause acute mortality, habitat disruption, and stock redistribution that reduce fishery reliability. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of marine heatwaves increases.

Deoxygenation contributes to fishery risk through habitat compression, mortality, and stock redistribution. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of oceanic deoxygenation.

Loss of trophic diversity weakens survival of young animals into adulthood and fishery resilience, while harvest outcomes remain management-dependent. Marine Food-Web Reorganization weakens by narrowing prey, habitat, and survival of young animals into adulthood processes.

Coastal hypoxia causes habitat compression, mortality, and fewer young animals surviving to adulthood that can collapse regional fisheries. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of coastal hypoxia.

Reef structural collapse raises risk of marine fisheries collapse through loss of nursery, shelter, and feeding habitat. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of reef structural collapse increases.
Carbon emissions warm and alter the ocean, shifting habitats and reducing the productivity of some fish populations. Fisheries can decline when species cannot adapt or move fast enough.

Large releases can injure commercially important fish and shellfish and close fisheries, with population outcomes depending on exposure, life stage, and recovery. A realized large petroleum release can injure fish and shellfish, damage supporting habitat and close fisheries.
outgoing: Fishery collapse or sustained stock decline reduces reliable landings, making supply disruption a direct operational expression of marine food-system stress. Shrinks through lower and less reliable catch.

Declining fishery availability raises food-security exposure where fish supplies a large share of dietary protein or household income. Marine Fisheries Collapse raises exposure for where diets and livelihoods depend heavily on fish.

A sustained decline in accessible stock can reduce expected catch and revenue, intensifying competition among fleets or states where access is contested and institutions cannot adjust allocation peacefully. The global predictor evidence is mixed and strong institutions, rebuilding plans, compensation, or alternative access can reduce pressure.

Selective removal of predators or consumers can change prey abundance and propagate effects across multiple feeding levels. Selective depletion of harvested predators or consumers can propagate through prey and lower trophic levels, but a trophic cascade requires measured intermediate and downstream responses rather than one declining taxon alone.

fish landing supply disruption.name: Fish Landing Supply Disruption
fish landing supply disruption.description: An interruption in the flow of harvested seafood from vessels to ports, processors, markets, and consumers. Landing disruption matters most where communities rely on fish as a major protein source, making dependence the exposed downstream condition.
incoming: Fishery collapse or sustained stock decline reduces reliable landings, making supply disruption a direct operational expression of marine food-system stress. Shrinks through lower and less reliable catch.

Food-web reorganization becomes socially visible when altered species composition and timing make local fish landings less reliable. Destabilizes when altered trophic structure reduces predictable catch composition and timing.

When pelagic species shift away from established grounds or seasons, local landing volumes and access can become more erratic even without outright collapse. The size of the change depends on the intensity and duration of pelagic species redistribution.

Many fisheries depend on predictable upwelling-supported productivity, so disrupted upwelling can quickly reduce catch reliability and landing stability. Destabilizes where catch depends on nutrient-fueled coastal productivity.

Reduced phytoplankton productivity can propagate up marine food webs and lower the reliability of fish landings in systems dependent on strong primary productivity. Erodes reliability of when food-web productivity falls at the base of marine harvest systems.

Nursery-habitat degradation can reduce future survival of young animals into adulthood and make small-scale and coastal fish landings less stable over time. Estuarine Nursery Loss reduces stability of when weaker juvenile survival of young animals into adulthood narrows future coastal catches.
Harmful blooms disrupt landings through fish kills, toxin accumulation, and precautionary harvest closures. The relationship grows stronger as the reach or duration of harmful algal blooms increases.

Low-oxygen events displace or kill stocks and directly disrupt the reliability of landings. Coastal hypoxia can disrupt fishery supply by causing mortality, compressing habitat or displacing target species and fishing effort.

Dense events can damage catches, clog nets and aquaculture enclosures, or interrupt coastal operations within the affected fishery. Named fishery, aquaculture site, or intake with event and operational records.
outgoing: Landing disruption matters most where communities rely on fish as a major protein source, making dependence the exposed downstream condition. The downstream effect depends on the geographic reach and persistence of fish landing supply disruption.
